pages.title: Kaspa Explained: What KAS Is, How GHOSTDAG Works, and What Is Live Now
pages.description: What KAS is, how the proof-of-work blockDAG and GHOSTDAG order blocks, and which Kaspa claims are live mainnet versus roadmap.
pages.text: Independent explainer What is Kaspa? Kaspa's miners work in parallel instead of racing for one slot. Every block that finds valid proof of work gets a place in a proof-of-work blockDAG rather than waiting to see if it survives a fork. GHOSTDAG is the rule that takes that graph, full of blocks mined at nearly the same time, and orders it into one payment history nodes agree on. Mainnet, testnet, roadmap, and open research get different labels here, because they carry different weights of evidence. None of them gets to borrow another one's proof. What is Kaspa? Network overview Proof of Work, blockDAG, GHOSTDAG, and KAS. Live now Current network status Mainnet facts, Toccata status, and dated checks. Check claims Run a claim through the labels Live, testnet, targeted, roadmap, research, wrong. Risks What can still break Adoption, liquidity, node load, mining, roadmap execution. Build Builder status Payments, Toccata rules, tooling, and vProgs later. Sources Primary documents Releases, KIPs, docs, APIs, papers, and repo links. Read What is Kaspa Check what is live Build on Kaspa New to crypto itself? Start with Start Here . Structure Losing blocks stay in the graph Rule GHOSTDAG orders history Boundary Fast inclusion, not instant finality Toccata status Toccata activation record Toccata is live. It activated at DAA score 474,165,565 under Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1, and mainnet now runs with L1 covenants, covenant IDs, ZK proof verification, sequencing commitments, and the based-app groundwork. Wallet support, explorer support, SDK coverage, and actual app usage sit on top of that protocol layer, but they are separate, still-building layers. Each one needs its own evidence, checked separately. Open Toccata Explained for what changes, Toccata status for the activation record, or Smart-Contract Status for app wording. Primary sources: Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 release and v2.0.0 activation release . Activation DAA 474,165,565 The score that flipped Toccata from testnet to live. Try next UTXO expressiveness Covenants, ZK checks, lanes, based apps, and vProgs boundaries. Capacity TPS of what? Payments, covenants, proofs, tokens, and future app throughput differ. Evidence Primary links Releases, KIPs, Testnet-10, vProgs, and Argent. BlockDAG model Compare the chain and the graph A single chain has to pick a winner: when two blocks arrive close together, one gets built on and the other is discarded, work and all. A blockDAG keeps both, links them into the graph as parents, and lets GHOSTDAG sort out the order afterward. Current view Kaspa blockDAG Choose the view Single chain BlockDAG Higher load Reader mode Plain Bitcoin user Builder Kaspa blockDAG Kaspa's losing blocks still count toward security. GHOSTDAG is the rule that turns the graph into one ordered payment history instead of throwing the losers away. Model Simulated Mainnet 10 BPS era Boundary Fast inclusion, not instant finality Network snapshot Current network numbers Pulled live from the public API for orientation. Cross-check anything that matters against a node, an explorer, or the source path below. If these numbers stop updating, they're stale, not proof of anything. Use Status and Sources for claims that need to hold up. Loading Circulating supply Loading Reported by `api.kaspa.org/info/coinsupply`. Mined Loading Circulating supply divided by max supply. DAG blocks Loading Total blocks in the blockDAG right now. DAA score Loading Kaspa's progress marker, roughly analogous to block height. Origin proof Kaspa.org publishes the fair-launch proof: an empty genesis UTXO set, Bitcoin timestamp anchors, checkpoint linkage, and scheduled emission starting from the Nov. 22, 2021 checkpoint. Verify on Kaspa.org Extra checks: run the proof , REST API docs , and DAGVIZ . Waiting for live data. Status Live, testnet, roadmap, research Four buckets, four different evidence bars. A claim moves up only when the evidence for that specific bucket shows up. Live 10 BPS PoW blockDAG Mining, UTXO ownership, GHOSTDAG, wallets, nodes, explorers. Testnet TN10/TN12 rehearsal Builder evidence before mainnet activation. Activation Toccata activation v2.0.0 sets DAA 474,165,565. Roadmap Apps that prove rules Richer app state, based apps, later vProgs, shared ordering. Risk What's still unproven Liquidity, node cost, mining concentration, fee demand, apps. Build path What can be built now? Moving money and verifying receipts are live today. Toccata adds covenant rules and proof-based app primitives to that surface. Now Move and inspect money Wallets, payments, receipts, exchange flows, mining/node visibility, and better confirmation-risk UX. Now Verify receipts Apps can show txid, amount, address, accepted status, source, timestamp, and fallback verification links. Toccata work Enforce spending rules Vault limits, delays, escrow, assurance contracts, asset rules, and bounded UTXO state machines are the near-term app surface. Later Prove richer app logic Markets, lending, funding rules, attestations, and shared commitments need richer app-state, custody, oracle, and proof paths. Build this now For the full path, open the builder guide . Transaction path Wallet to confirmation Five steps from signed transaction to a history nodes won't reorganize away. 1 Create Wallet prepares inputs, outputs, amount, and fee. 2 Broadcast The transaction reaches nodes and miners. 3 Mine A miner includes it in a proof-of-work block. 4 Order The block joins the DAG and GHOSTDAG orders history. 5 Confirm Confidence rises as more accepted work piles on top of it. pages.title: Start Here | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: A beginner-first start page for Kaspa Explained: learn crypto from zero, then understand coins, market value, tradeoffs, and where Kaspa fits.
pages.text: Start here Start with the problem Every crypto mechanism answers the same question: what breaks if you remove the one trusted operator? This path starts with records, then works through keys, transactions, blocks, consensus, incentives, markets, coin categories, tradeoffs, and finally Kaspa. Kaspa mental model parallel blocks, one spend history Mined blocks can appear in parallel and still land in one ordered history. Forget the single-file line: that's the wrong picture here. Content plan What this guide teaches This is the beginner syllabus. It starts with plain mental models, then separates live mainnet behavior from testnet evidence, roadmap work, and claims Kaspa isn't making yet. One sentence Kaspa is a mined Proof-of-Work blockDAG where GHOSTDAG orders parallel blocks into one shared payment history. The normal tradeoff Most chains trade off between slower global ordering, more centralization pressure, or more complex execution and network assumptions. blockDAG analogy Instead of forcing honest blocks into one slow line, Kaspa keeps parallel work visible in a graph and orders it afterward. GHOSTDAG ordering GHOSTDAG is the ordering rule that lets nodes agree on which parallel blocks belong in the selected history. Confirmations Fast inclusion isn't instant finality. Confirmations track growing confidence that a transaction stays in the accepted history. BPS BPS means blocks per second. Crescendo-era 10 BPS is live; throughput, TPS, and confirmation behavior each need their own precise wording. Crescendo, Toccata, KIPs Crescendo is the live 10 BPS era. Toccata, KIPs, covenants, and sequencing commitments each carry their own status. Live versus future Mainnet behavior, testnet evidence, targeted hard-fork work, roadmap architecture, and research are five different claim types here. Use cases High-throughput mined ordering fits payments, receipts, wallets, proofs, custody, and later rule-based app workflows. Not claiming yet Live native DeFi, live DAGKnight, live vProgs, instant finality, and automatic adoption are not current Kaspa claims. 1 · Problem What is Kaspa trying to solve? The compressed thesis: fast mined ordering without turning into one operator's database. 2 · Live status What is live? Mainnet behavior versus testnet proofs, roadmap, research, and app claims outside L1 scope. 3 · Risk What could go wrong? The strongest objections: node pressure, security budget, liquidity, mining concentration, tooling fragility, and roadmap execution. I know nothing Crypto from zero. Digital records, keys, transactions, blocks, consensus, tokens, and tradeoffs, from the start. I see hundreds of coins Why so many coins exist. Bitcoin-like money, smart-contract platforms, stablecoins, exchange tokens, privacy coins, memes, DeFi, and infrastructure are not the same thing. I want value explained Why crypto has prices. Token need, market cap, liquidity, security budget, speculation, launch design, and why price alone proves nothing. I want the constraints The tradeoff map. Why speed, privacy, decentralization, security, funding, open markets, and node requirements pull against each other. I want examples Coin atlas. BTC, ETH, SOL, XRP, BNB, stablecoins, LTC, BCH, XMR, DOGE, LINK, and KAS, sorted by category. I want a checklist Analyze any coin. Does the token need to exist? Who got supply first, who secures it, what can fail, and who benefits? The beginner promise What each page is for Problem What breaks in a normal digital system? Copying, double-spending, operator control, spam, censorship, privacy leakage, coordination failure. Mechanism What tool answers it? Keys, signatures, transactions, blocks, consensus, mining, staking, fees, tokens, markets. Tradeoff What cost shows up? Hardware, latency, complexity, user responsibility, public data, volatility, centralization pressure, funding problems. Kaspa Once the general mechanism is clear, ask where Kaspa fits: PoW, UTXO, blockDAG, GHOSTDAG, fair launch, and the app work still being built. Best route Beginner reading order Digital ownership is hard. Digital information copies for free, so a scarce digital asset needs explicit rules for uniqueness and spending. Records need an accepted authority. A bank, platform, exchange, or public network has to decide which updates count. Crypto removes the easy operator. That trade creates new problems: keys, validation, ordering, spam, incentives, security, privacy, scaling, governance. Consensus is the shared-history problem. Independent computers need to land on one accepted state even when messages arrive in different orders. Tokens are part of the incentive system. They track value, pay fees, reward miners or validators, fund security, and attract speculation. Coins differ because problems differ. Bitcoin, Ethereum, stablecoins, Solana, BNB, XRP, Monero, Dogecoin, Chainlink, and Kaspa are not the same kind of thing. Kaspa is the destination here. Kaspa's bet: a mined shared record can feel closer to real time without turning into a normal centralized database. Quick corrections Common beginner mistakes A coin is not automatically cheap because the unit price is low Supply changes the comparison. Market cap, float, liquidity, access, adoption, and demand carry more signal than what one unit costs. Fast is not the same as final Inclusion, confirmation, finality, throughput, and wallet UX are separate layers of "speed." Decentralized does not mean no one has influence Mining, staking, nodes, developers, exchanges, wallets, foundations, RPC providers, and market makers each create their own concentration points. Crypto is not one market Stablecoins, smart-contract platforms, exchange tokens, privacy coins, meme coins, governance tokens, and PoW money assets are different instruments entirely. pages.description: What is Kaspa? KAS, Proof of Work, blockDAGs, GHOSTDAG, 10 BPS, and what's live on mainnet versus still roadmap.
pages.text: Beginner answer What is Kaspa? Kaspa is a live proof-of-work blockDAG network. It keeps Bitcoin-style mining and UTXO ownership, and uses GHOSTDAG to order parallel blocks into one payment history. Summary: Kaspa is a mined UTXO blockDAG. GHOSTDAG takes parallel proof-of-work blocks and turns them into one ordered payment history. The limits matter too: the Risks and Open Questions page covers adoption, liquidity, mining concentration, node load, security budget, and roadmap execution. Plain model The simple picture Coin KAS is the native coin people send, receive, mine, and pay fees with. Security Kaspa runs on Proof of Work. Miners spend real energy, hardware, and operating time to produce each block. Ownership Kaspa uses UTXOs: wallets spend specific outputs, not a running account balance. Shape Kaspa's ledger is a blockDAG. Two honest blocks found seconds apart both stay in the graph instead of one being discarded. Ordering GHOSTDAG is the rule nodes use to turn that graph into one shared payment history. Status The live network runs at 10 BPS in the Crescendo era. Future app and consensus work carries its own, separate status label. Live vs next What is live, and what is not live? Claim Status Safer wording Kaspa is Proof of Work Live Kaspa is mined Proof of Work. Kaspa is 10 BPS Live Kaspa runs at 10 BPS in the Crescendo era. July 2026 is a sudden emission cliff Misleading Emission steps down monthly. July 2026 is one scheduled step, not a cliff. Toccata has activated on mainnet Activated Toccata crossed its mainnet activation score. That protocol switch is live; app, wallet, explorer, and SDK support still need their own checks. DAGKnight is current mainnet consensus Research DAGKnight is research and implementation work, not deployed. Current mainnet consensus is GHOSTDAG. pages.title: Crypto From Zero | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: Crypto from zero: why digital ownership is hard, why records need rules, why keys, transactions, blocks, consensus, mining, staking, tokens, and tradeoffs exist.
pages.text: Crypto from zero Crypto starts with shared records Money, balances, tickets, game items, stablecoins, and crypto all depend on records. The hard question was never storage. It is who can change the record, who checks the change, and why everyone else has to accept it. Crypto keeps one shared digital record without one trusted operator. Remove the operator and you inherit their old job: keys, consensus, incentives, markets, and group action all have to be rebuilt from scratch. The ladder From zero to Kaspa 1 Records Who owns what? Who paid whom? Which update happened first? 2 Keys A private key lets a user authorize updates without asking a platform login server. 3 Transactions A transaction is a signed instruction asking the shared record to change. 4 Blocks A block packages valid updates into a proposed piece of shared history. 5 Consensus Independent computers need rules for which history counts when updates conflict. 6 Incentives Unknown operators need reasons to follow rules and costs for attacking them. 7 Markets Tokens trade because users, miners, validators, investors, and apps need entry and exit. 8 Kaspa Kaspa keeps PoW and UTXO design, then uses a blockDAG to reduce the single-chain bottleneck. Layer 0 Why digital ownership is hard Physical cash has location Hand someone a banknote and you no longer hold it. The physical object cannot sit in two wallets at once: scarcity is a property of matter, free of charge. Digital data copies for free A file copies. A database row edits. A screenshot duplicates. None of that scarcity survives the jump to bits, so digital money has to manufacture it with rules instead of physics. Beginner summary: Coins do not fly through the internet. A valid transaction changes an accepted record, and that record is the whole asset. Trusted operator Why a bank database is simpler Most systems solve the ownership problem with an operator. A bank, exchange, payment app, or platform runs the database and decides which updates count. One authority fixing mistakes, blocking fraud, reversing payments, and pushing upgrades is a cheaper design than the alternative, right up until you need something the authority won't give you. Operator model What it gives you What it can cost Bank or payment app Customer support, reversals, fraud handling, legal recourse. Account freezes, censorship, operating hours, jurisdiction limits, counterparty risk. Exchange or platform Fast internal balances and easy UX. Custody risk, hidden liabilities, withdrawal risk, policy changes. Public crypto network Rules can be checked by independent participants. More complexity, irreversible mistakes, public data, slower coordination. Why cryptography Crypto needs proof without a login desk Private key The secret that controls spending authority. Steal it and the network cannot tell the thief from the owner: there is no ID check behind the math. Public key or address Lets anyone verify a signature is valid without ever seeing the private key that produced it. Signature Proof that the key holder authorized this specific transaction. It stands in for the username, password, and account admin a normal platform would use. Hash A fingerprint for data. Change one byte of the input and the fingerprint changes completely, which is what lets a block chain to its history and makes tampering visible. What breaks without keys: the system falls back on a central login authority or an identity registry to decide who can move a balance. Transactions and blocks Why transactions and blocks exist Transaction A signed instruction: spend this value, create that new value, pay this fee. Every field in it exists so a stranger's node can check it without asking the sender anything else. Why it exists: the network needs one precise object to validate, not a conversation. Block A batch of valid transactions linked to prior history. Nodes either accept the whole batch under the protocol's rules or reject it. There is no partial credit. Why it exists: the network needs a shared unit of history that a majority can agree happened. Consensus Why records need agreement A record is only worth something if strangers agree it's the record. Show Bob one ledger and Carol another and you've just spent the same coin twice. Consensus exists because thousands of independent computers see network messages arrive in different orders, and they still have to converge on one shared state anyway. Which transaction came first? Which block counts? Was the same value spent twice? Did a miner or validator follow the rules? Can history be rewritten cheaply? Can users verify the supply? Security Security means the record resists lies Attack Plain meaning Why users care Theft Spend value without the rightful key holder's consent. Ownership is meaningless if signatures can be forged or keys are stolen. Double-spend Try to spend the same value in two conflicting ways. Recipients need to know which payment counts. Rewrite Replace accepted history with a different history. Settlement needs confidence that old payments stay settled. Censorship Prevent valid transactions from entering history. Open access fails if a control point can cheaply block users. Hidden inflation Create value outside the rules. Supply rules work only if users can independently reject invalid supply. Mining and staking Consensus has to cost something Proof of Work PoW prices out fake history with a cost outside the system: hardware, electricity, time. Miners propose blocks and get paid only if that work sticks in accepted history. Tradeoff: energy use, ASICs, mining pools, industrial concentration pressure. Proof of Stake PoS prices out fake history with a cost inside the system: validators post the native asset as collateral and can lose it for provable bad behavior, depending on the design. Tradeoff: wealth concentration, delegation, staking-provider power, harder social-recovery questions when things go wrong. Tokens Why public networks often use tokens A permissionless network needs some internal economic unit to price fees, pay rewards, resist spam, and fund its own security. Wanting a token is not the same as needing one. Object tracked The ledger records ownership of the asset itself. Fee asset Users pay for scarce block space and avoid free spam. Security reward Miners or validators are paid to operate and defend the system. Market entry Open markets let users, miners, validators, apps, and investors enter or exit without one issuer approving every participant. Simple check: most tokens don't need to exist. Ask what this one does that BTC, ETH, USDC, or a plain database doesn't already do. UTXO and account models Two ways to track state Account model A balance table. Alice has 10, sends 3, and now Alice has 7 while Bob has 3. Intuitive, and the default for smart-contract platforms, until two transactions touch the same shared balance at once and ordering starts to matter. UTXO model More like cash notes than a ledger. Alice spends a 10-coin output, Bob receives a 3-coin output, Alice receives a 7-coin change output, and the original 10-coin note is gone for good. Kaspa uses a UTXO model, same as Bitcoin. That single choice shapes how validation works, how much can run in parallel, and what shape future programmability can even take. UTXO intuition: the old output is consumed once. New outputs carry the next spendable state. Kaspa appears here Where Kaspa enters Bitcoin-style chains pick one block path at a time and throw away the rest. That's conservative and it works, but it caps how fast blocks can arrive: two honest miners who solve a block seconds apart start competing instead of both counting. Kaspa's bet is that a mined UTXO network can keep both blocks, order them with GHOSTDAG instead of discarding one, and get payments closer to real time without changing what PoW is securing. Kaspa design case Where Kaspa fits What is live Next step Understand value and coin categories next Mechanics explain how a record changes hands. They don't explain why a token has a price, or why Bitcoin and Ethereum aren't competing for the same job. Why crypto has value Open coin atlas Keep reading Next pages Previous What is Kaspa? pages.title: Why Crypto Has Value | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: Why cryptoassets have prices: token need, market cap, liquidity, security budget, speculation, launch design, open markets, and why price is not proof.
pages.text: Market value Why crypto has value A token price is smoke. The question is what's burning underneath it. Sometimes it's a real engine: usage, scarce block space, a security budget miners actually depend on, collateral demand. Sometimes it's culture, leverage, or an insider exit dressed up as a chart. Native token Why a token may be necessary Role What it does Beginner warning Thing being tracked The ledger defines and transfers the asset itself. A token can exist without being useful outside speculation. Fees Users pay for scarce block space and spam resistance. Low fees help UX but can weaken fee revenue or invite spam. Security budget Miners or validators need compensation for defending the record. Rewards may come from inflation, fees, or both. Collateral Some systems require staked tokens or bonded assets. Capital-based security can concentrate around large holders and custodians. Governance Some tokens vote on parameters, treasuries, or upgrades. Governance rights can be weak, captured, or mostly symbolic. Price Why cryptoassets get prices Demand for use Someone needs the asset itself: to pay fees, settle a trade, stake, post collateral, or get into an app. Monetary premium Markets pay extra for credible scarcity, liquidity, durability, and censorship resistance backed by a rule set people trust enough not to check twice. Security economics Higher rewards buy more mining or staking security, and a higher market value makes the network a more tempting target to attack or capture. Speculation Markets price in expectations, narrative, attention, and leverage. Price rises because people expect price to rise; that loop can run for a long time before it needs a reason. Rule: a price pump is not proof of adoption. A high market cap is not proof of usefulness. A technically sound project can still be overpriced. Market cap Market cap is not company value Market cap is price times circulating supply, nothing more. It does not mean that much cash actually flowed into the asset, it proves no revenue, and it does not mean holders could sell at that price if they tried. Price per coin means nothing without supply attached. Circulating supply can differ sharply from total supply. Low float inflates paper valuations without a matching amount of real capital. Volume can mean liquidity, hype, wash trading, or panic: the number alone doesn't say which. Social dominance measures attention, not fundamentals. Those need separate evidence. Fully diluted value shows the dilution still coming. Kaspa/BTC example: one KAS costs less than one BTC because there are far more of them, not because it's "cheaper." Compare market cap, liquidity, access, adoption, security history, and execution risk instead of unit price. Open markets Open markets and their costs Why markets help Miners and validators can sell rewards. Users can acquire the fee asset. Apps can price collateral and liquidity. Global participants can enter and exit without one issuer. Security budget gets a market signal. What markets break Pump-and-dumps become easy to coordinate. Insiders can use retail liquidity as exit liquidity. Leverage can force violent liquidations. Narrative can outrun working technology. Price can dominate the education layer. Ponzi or not Risk and fraud Trading in an open market where early buyers profit does not make an asset a Ponzi. What does: promising guaranteed returns, paying yield out of new deposits instead of revenue, hiding who holds the supply, or building something that mainly exists so insiders have someone to sell to. Not enough to call fraud Volatility, early gains, speculation, or the absence of an obvious consumer app. Red flags Guaranteed yield, hidden insiders, vague utility, unlock cliffs, fake partnerships, opaque reserves, no working system. Price is not legitimacy A meme can reach a large valuation on attention alone. A technically sound network can sit ignored for years. Launch design Initial ownership shapes trust Launch model What it improves What it risks Fair launch / mined launch Lower official insider-allocation risk. No built-in treasury, early-miner advantage, harder funding. Premine Funds development, legal work, grants, audits, and integrations. Insider control, sell pressure, trust problems. Public sale or ICO Fast fundraising and broad early buyer base. Regulatory risk, hype buying, weak product discipline. VC allocation Professional funding and business support. Unlock overhang and retail exit-liquidity risk. Airdrop Rewards users and broadens distribution. Farming, sybil attacks, immediate sell pressure. A fair launch removes the official allocation table. It does not remove the funding, coordination, early-miner, liquidity, or ecosystem-development questions that a premine would have paid for. Who is in the game Different actors value different things Actor What they usually care about Users Payments, apps, custody, privacy, low fees, and safety. Traders Liquidity, volatility, momentum, listings, and narratives. Miners Rewards, fees, hardware efficiency, electricity cost, and mining difficulty. Validators and stakers Yield, uptime, slashing risk, delegation, and governance influence. Developers Tooling, grants, users, technical influence, and protocol stability. Exchanges and market makers Trading volume, custody, liquidity, spreads, and listing demand. Funds and insiders Entry price, liquidity, unlocks, exits, and narrative timing. Regulators Market integrity, tax, AML controls, disclosures, consumer risk, and systemic risk. Next step Now separate coin categories BTC, ETH, USDT, XRP, BNB, SOL, DOGE, LINK, LTC, BCH, XMR, and KAS get ranked on the same leaderboard and priced in the same units. They are not the same kind of asset. The coin atlas starts there. pages.title: Why Are There So Many Coins? | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: Why there are so many crypto coins: different problems, trust models, tokens, markets, forks, stablecoins, exchange tokens, memes, privacy, DeFi, and Kaspa.
pages.text: Coin categories Why there are many coins Bitcoin is scarce digital money. Ethereum runs programmable apps. Solana chases on-chain speed. Stablecoins move dollars on a public ledger instead of a bank's. Monero sells privacy. BNB is tied to one exchange's ecosystem. Meme coins turn attention itself into a market. Kaspa tests mined money that feels closer to real time. None of them are competing for the same job. That is why there are thousands of coins instead of one winner. One list, many instruments Market tables mix categories Sort a ranking page by market cap and BTC, ETH, USDT, XRP, BNB, SOL, DOGE, LINK, LTC, BCH, XMR, wrapped assets, stablecoins, and meme tokens all land in one column. Same units, same table, completely different products: a scarcity play, a fee-driven platform, a dollar substitute, and an attention market, ranked as if they compete for the same job. Category Examples What it is selling Main risk Bitcoin-like money BTC, LTC, BCH, KAS Scarce transfer and settlement assets. Weak app demand, fee pressure, or lower security budget. Smart-contract platforms ETH, SOL, AVAX, SUI Programmable blockspace and app ecosystems. Scaling complexity, validator concentration, app speculation. Stablecoins USDT, USDC, DAI, PYUSD Dollar-like units on crypto networks. Issuer, reserve, depeg, censorship, and banking risk. Exchange tokens BNB, OKB, CRO, LEO Exchange ecosystem access, fees, burns, or chain gas. Company dependence and regulatory pressure. Payment and enterprise rails XRP, XLM, HBAR, XDC Fast settlement, enterprise rails, or tokenization narratives. Adoption may not require token appreciation. Privacy coins XMR, ZEC, DASH Financial privacy and fungibility. Heavier cryptography, regulation, and liquidity pressure. Meme coins Attention-driven assets Culture, attention, liquidity, and speculation. Narrative collapse and insider concentration. Infrastructure tokens LINK, PYTH, GRT, FIL Data, storage, indexing, or oracle services. Value capture may be unclear. Why new coins appear Different reasons coins exist Different design answers PoW versus PoS, UTXO versus account model, privacy versus transparency, execution speed versus low node requirements, L1 versus L2. Each pick trades away something the other kept, so no single design wins on every axis at once. Different social goals Digital gold, peer-to-peer cash, private payments, DeFi apps, enterprise settlement, exchange ecosystems, games, identity, storage, coordination. Forks and disagreements Communities split when they can't agree on scaling, governance, monetary rules, or what the project is even supposed to be. Speculation incentives A new token attracts liquidity and attention on its own, independent of whether the network needed a token at all. Beginner frame Ask what the coin is trying to be Money or settlement asset? App platform? Dollar token? Exchange ecosystem token? Privacy tool? Governance token? Infrastructure network? Attention market? Claim on an off-chain asset? Why value differs High or low market value can come from many causes Why a coin may be highly valued Deep liquidity and exchange access. A narrative simple enough to repeat in one sentence. A large developer or app ecosystem. A community with real social consensus behind it. Staking, fee, collateral, or security demand. Institutional familiarity or regulatory clarity. Speculative attention and leverage. Why good tech may stay low-valued Weak liquidity or exchange access. No narrative simple enough to spread. A token that fails to capture the value the network creates. A small developer ecosystem. Funding and business-development gaps. Bad timing, bad UX, or stronger competitors. A market that hasn't priced the tradeoff yet. pages.description: A beginner coin atlas: Bitcoin, Ethereum, stablecoins, Solana, BNB, XRP, Litecoin, Bitcoin Cash, Monero, Dogecoin, Chainlink, and Kaspa by category and tradeoff.
pages.text: Coin atlas Major coins by job Bitcoin, a stablecoin, and a meme coin can sit next to each other on a market-cap chart, ranked by the same number. That number says nothing about what any of them do. Scarce money, programmable execution, a dollar peg, and pure attention are different products competing for the same spot on a list. Why so many coins? Analyze any coin Value stack What each coin mostly offers Asset or category What it tries to be Why markets may value it Main limitation Bitcoin Scarce neutral money and final-record asset. Liquidity, history, PoW security, fixed-supply culture, social consensus. Slow base layer, limited app rules, fee pressure, no privacy by default. Ethereum Programmable app and final-record platform. DeFi, stablecoins, developer network, gas, staking, L2 settlement. Complex roadmap, L2 fragmentation, MEV, staking concentration risk. Stablecoins Dollar-like units on crypto networks. Trading liquidity, payments, DeFi collateral, cross-border dollar access. Issuer, reserve, censorship, depeg, and banking risk. Solana High-speed smart-contract platform. Fast UX, low fees, apps, DEX activity, retail culture, developer attention. Performance can increase hardware and coordination pressure. BNB Exchange-linked ecosystem asset. Exchange user base, chain gas, burns, incentives, liquidity. Company and regulatory dependence. XRP Payment rail asset. Long history, liquidity, community, fast ledger settlement, enterprise narrative. Token demand can be separate from enterprise software adoption. Litecoin Legacy Bitcoin-like payment coin. Age, liquidity, simple design, faster blocks than Bitcoin, broad exchange support. Less differentiated in a world with stablecoins, L2s, and many fast chains. Bitcoin Cash Bigger-block peer-to-peer cash branch. Bitcoin lineage, low-fee on-chain payment philosophy, committed community. Weaker network effect and security budget than BTC. Monero Privacy-first payment network. Fungibility, censorship resistance, real privacy demand, ideological commitment. Regulatory pressure, exchange delistings, heavier data and verification tradeoffs. Dogecoin and memes Attention and community markets. Culture, liquidity, virality, exchange access, speculative Schelling point. Weak technical necessity and extreme narrative risk. Chainlink and oracles Data infrastructure for smart contracts. DeFi dependency, price feeds, integrations, infrastructure network effects. Token value capture and oracle centralization questions. Kaspa Fast Proof-of-Work UTXO blockDAG. PoW, fair launch, blockDAG thesis, faster confirmation feel, community, roadmap optionality. App layer, liquidity, adoption, security budget, and roadmap execution still decide the case. Trust model Sort assets by what you have to trust No single issuer, PoW-style money BTC, LTC, BCH, XMR, and KAS have no company behind the token: miners secure the network directly. The risk lives in mining economics, node validation, liquidity depth, and whether the security budget holds up as issuance drops. Smart-contract platforms ETH, SOL, AVAX, SUI, ADA, and BNB Chain sell programmable state. The token pays for compute and storage; it doesn't function as money on its own. The risk is execution scale under load, validator concentration, bridge exploits, and whether developers keep shipping there next year. Issuer-backed assets USDT, USDC, PYUSD, tokenized gold, and tokenized stocks are only as good as the entity standing behind them. Reserves, redemption rights, banking access, and jurisdiction sit upstream of the token: those are what to check. Governance and protocol tokens UNI, AAVE, MKR/SKY, COMP, and CRV vote on protocol parameters, treasuries, or fees. One question decides whether that vote is worth anything: does the governance control real economic value, or just settings nobody profits from changing? Wrapped and liquid staking assets WBTC, cbBTC, stETH, rETH, and JitoSOL are claims on an underlying asset held somewhere else. Every layer of composability adds a layer of risk: custodian, bridge, smart-contract bug, depeg, rehypothecation. Attention assets A meme coin is worth something because attention itself trades. That's the entire mechanism: no protocol, no cash flow, no redemption right underneath it. Coin profile template A plain explanation checklist What problem does it solve? What type of asset is it? Why does the token need to exist? Who secures it? Who validates it? Who got supply first? What drives demand? What could make value fall? What should beginners not misunderstand? Kaspa bridge Where Kaspa fits in the atlas Kaspa sits in the PoW monetary-network branch with Bitcoin, Litecoin, and Bitcoin Cash, but it drops the single-chain block structure. Blocks form a DAG instead of a chain, and GHOSTDAG orders them: that ordering mechanism is behind Kaspa's faster confirmation feel. It is not a stablecoin, an exchange token, a meme coin, or a live smart-contract platform. Judge it on the terms that apply to a PoW money network: mining security, fair launch, blockDAG throughput, liquidity depth, node requirements, and whether mined payments that settle faster than Bitcoin actually solve a problem someone has. pages.title: Crypto Tradeoff Map | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: A beginner crypto tradeoff map: speed, security, decentralization, privacy, scaling, nodes, ASICs, staking, token launches, fees, markets, and Kaspa.
pages.text: Tradeoff map Crypto design has tradeoffs No crypto design solves speed, security, decentralization, and privacy at once. Push on one and the cost shows up somewhere else: hardware requirements, bandwidth, latency, regulatory exposure, funding structure, or who actually controls the network. Speed feedback Security cost Many verifiers decentralization Privacy hidden data Usability recovery A design can improve one corner, but the pressure moves somewhere else. Tradeoff intuition: the question is never whether a feature is good. It's where the cost lands once the feature is added. Master map What people want and what it costs Goal Why people want it What it costs Decentralization No easy single control point. Harder upgrades, worse UX, slower coordination, more user responsibility. Security Hard-to-fake history and valid supply. Fees, energy, staked capital, complexity, and security-budget pressure. Speed Fast inclusion and better user feedback. Propagation pressure, node requirements, weaker verification, or centralization risk. Privacy Less surveillance and better fungibility. More cryptography, heavier data, harder auditability, lower exchange access. Self-custody Direct control without a platform account. No simple password reset, chargeback, or customer-service recovery. Open access Anyone can join, transact, build, mine, validate, or exit. Spam, scams, hostile actors, bots, and manipulation. Fair launch Lower official insider-allocation risk. Harder funding, slower business development, early-miner advantage. Funded launch More money for development, audits, grants, legal work, and integrations. Insider allocation, unlocks, sell pressure, and governance capture. Visa question Why crypto differs from Visa Visa settles fast because Visa doesn't ask for independent verification. Trusted institutions, legal agreements, one company's infrastructure, and fraud teams do the work instead. A public blockchain asks many independent participants to check the same rules without trusting any single operator. That redundant verification is the bottleneck Visa doesn't have. Normal app or payment network Runs on infrastructure one company controls. That operator can optimize for speed, reverse errors, block users, and change rules whenever it wants. Public crypto base layer Independent nodes can reject invalid history without asking permission. The cost of that guarantee: data, execution, and ordering all have to stay verifiable by people outside any one company. Beginner summary: crypto can look Visa-fast at the app or custody layer. A decentralized base layer can't, without quietly picking up Visa's trust assumptions along the way. Scaling Bigger or faster has costs Scaling method What it improves What it risks Bigger blocks More transactions per block. Heavier bandwidth, storage, and node requirements. Faster blocks Faster inclusion and better UX. More propagation conflict and consensus complexity. Parallel execution More app throughput. More complex state management and developer assumptions. Rollups More execution away from L1. Sequencer, bridge, proof, and data-availability complexity. Payment channels Fast cheap repeated payments. Liquidity management and routing complexity. Centralized custody Best speed and recovery UX. Trust the operator again. Privacy Privacy and public verification conflict Public chains expose transaction data because independent verifiers need that data to check the rules. Hiding sender, receiver, amount, or app state solves privacy and creates new cost: heavier cryptography, bigger data, harder verification, thinner liquidity, and more regulatory friction. Transparent ledgers Easy to audit supply and verify rules. Bad for user privacy and business confidentiality. Privacy-first systems Better fungibility, less surveillance. Harder exchange access, heavier data, more regulatory pressure. Shielding has limits Worth having. It doesn't remove the scaling, compliance, UX, and verification costs underneath it. Hardware ASICs and staking are different concentration pressures ASIC mining Specialized machines put real-world cost into PoW security: electricity, hardware, facilities, cooling, supply chains, geography, time. That cost doesn't prevent concentration. It just moves it to whoever controls capital, cheap energy, chip manufacturing, firmware, and pools. Staking PoS skips industrial hardware entirely: the security resource is token ownership itself. Concentration risk moves accordingly, to large holders, staking providers, exchanges, liquid-staking protocols, and governance votes. Kaspa relevance Kaspa's tradeoff is fast PoW Kaspa's specific bet: keep PoW and UTXO design while using a blockDAG and GHOSTDAG ordering to include parallel honest blocks instead of discarding them, improving confirmation feel. That bet does not cancel node economics, mining economics, app-layer challenges, privacy tradeoffs, market volatility, or roadmap execution risk. They still apply, same as any other chain. Next step Apply the tradeoffs The coin atlas shows how different assets picked different constraints. The Kaspa comparison page shows exactly where fast PoW fits into that picture. pages.description: A beginner checklist for analyzing any crypto coin: token need, supply, launch, security, validators, miners, liquidity, market cap, risks, and who benefits.
pages.text: Checklist How to analyze a coin Token necessity, supply, launch design, security, validation, liquidity, market structure, and the strongest criticism against it: check those first. Price is the last thing to look at, not the first. The 20 questions Start with these questions What problem does it solve? Why does the token need to exist, specifically? Could BTC, ETH, USDC, or a plain database do the same job? Who pays the fees, and for what? Who secures it: miners, validators, or a company? Who validates it, and how many independent parties can? Who can change the rules, and under what process? How did it launch: mined, sold, airdropped, or allocated? Who got early supply, and how much? Are there unlocks still coming, and when? What gives it durable demand beyond speculation? What pays for security once early incentives fade? What does it cost to run a node? What part of the system is actually centralized? What is private, and what is public by design? What would make the token unnecessary tomorrow? What is the specific failure mode? What would have to be true to justify the market cap? What is the strongest argument against it? Who profits if retail buys in right now? Token necessity Classify the token first Classification What it means Common examples Necessary native asset Remove the token and the network stops functioning: it pays fees, pays rewards, and secures the chain in one move. BTC, ETH, KAS, SOL in their own network contexts. Helpful but optional The token coordinates incentives or access, but a different asset could plausibly fill the same role without breaking the design. Some app, infrastructure, and ecosystem tokens. Governance-only token Value depends entirely on whether the governance vote controls real fees, parameters, or treasury funds, or just cosmetic settings. Many DeFi protocol tokens. Claim or wrapper The token represents something else held elsewhere. Its value rests on redemption rights, custody, bridge security, and contract trust, not the token itself. Wrapped BTC, liquid staking tokens, tokenized gold or stocks. Attention token Culture and tradable attention are the entire value proposition, with no underlying mechanism required. Meme coins. Likely unnecessary An existing asset or a normal database could run the same product with no loss of function. Many weak utility tokens. Green and red flags Fast risk scan Green flags A one-sentence answer for why the token has to exist, not just what it does. Supply and launch history that anyone can check against on-chain data. Active commits and documentation a stranger can read without an NDA. Someone outside the founding team can run a validator or node and actually verify state. Liquidity deep enough to exit a real position, with no unlock cliff dumping new supply at once. Users who come back a second time, not just a first airdrop claim. The team names its own weak points before a critic does. Red flags Any promise of guaranteed yield or "no risk": yield without risk does not exist. Insiders hold most of the supply while public float stays thin. Partnerships that don't show up in the partner's own announcements. No answer for why this needs a token instead of a database row. Reserves, custody, bridges, or admin keys that nobody outside the team can inspect. Influencer campaigns running well before there's a working product to campaign for. Terms like "ecosystem," "unlock," or "infrastructure" doing the work a mechanism should do. Market table How to read a coin-ranking page Field What it means What can mislead Price The cost of one unit of the token. A $0.001 token is not "cheap." Divide by total supply before comparing it to anything. Market cap Price multiplied by circulating supply. It measures none of the following: revenue, capital actually invested, or how much of that value could be sold without crashing the price. Volume Amount traded over a given period. Real liquidity, panic selling, hype buying, and wash trading all show up as the same number. Circulating supply Tokens counted as available to trade. "Circulating" does not mean "not controlled by insiders." Large blocks can sit with early holders and still count. FDV Price multiplied by total possible supply, including tokens not yet unlocked. A market cap that looks small next to a much larger FDV is a dilution warning, not a bargain. Social dominance Share of crypto social-media attention. Attention is not adoption, and it is not durable. It can vanish in a week. Category labels Tags a market site assigns for search and filtering. Often too broad, stale, promotional, or wrong about the actual mechanism. Kaspa lens Apply it to Kaspa KAS clears the token-necessity question more easily than most app tokens do: it is the asset a PoW UTXO blockDAG network tracks, charges fees in, and pays out as the mining reward. Remove KAS and there's no network left underneath it. The fair launch means no official insider allocation to discount for. That does not answer the rest of the checklist: liquidity, security budget, mining concentration, node requirements, adoption, funding, app-layer execution, and roadmap status are still open questions with their own evidence, not settled by the launch design. pages.title: Crypto History as Problems | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: Crypto history explained as a sequence of problems: digital cash, Bitcoin, mining, ASICs, Ethereum, ICOs, scaling wars, DeFi, stablecoins, rollups, and Kaspa.
pages.text: History Crypto history as problem solving Every era of crypto history is a workaround for the era before it. Digital scarcity forced double-spend protection. Double-spend protection forced mining economics. Mining economics forced scaling fights, which forced rollups and new consensus designs. Read it as a chain of constraints, not a highlight reel. Problem timeline Problems by era Before Bitcoin Digital cash Digital data copies for free. Every pre-Bitcoin proposal had to fake the scarcity that atoms get automatically. Bitcoin Double-spending Proof of Work made rewriting a shared payment history expensive enough that no financial institution had to referee it. Early mining Security market Mining rewards turned CPUs into GPUs, GPUs into ASICs, and solo miners into pools and industrial operations chasing the same margin. Litecoin and forks Parameter experiments Communities forked Bitcoin's code to change one dial at a time: block times, mining algorithm, or scaling philosophy. Ethereum Programmability A ledger that runs code, not just balances: shared state any application could read and write. 2017 ICOs and scaling war Fundraising ran ahead of working products while Bitcoin's own community split over how to scale it. DeFi and stablecoins On-chain finance Dollar tokens, exchanges, lending, collateral, and automated market makers became the actual usage, not the demo. Rollups and fast L1s Scale and UX Execution moved off the base chain, into L2s, high-throughput L1s, appchains, and new consensus designs built to avoid the same bottleneck twice. Forks Software plus social agreement A company ships an update and users get it whether they like it or not. Crypto has no such lever: users, miners or validators, exchanges, wallets, and businesses all have to independently choose to run the new rules. A fork is what happens when they stop converging. Soft-fork style change Tightens the rules. Upgraded nodes enforce new restrictions while un-upgraded nodes still see the resulting blocks as valid. Hard-fork style change Changes the rules in a way old software rejects outright. Sometimes planned and boring, sometimes the moment a community splits in two. Bitcoin dominance Bitcoin as the reference point Bitcoin's value case rests on fixed-supply culture, PoW security, liquidity, exchange support, over a decade of surviving attacks, conservative upgrades, and a monetary story simple enough to repeat in one sentence. The tradeoff for that conservatism: no fast retail-speed L1 UX, no expressive smart contracts, no easy experimentation. Why other chains exist Different projects, different pressures Bitcoin Cash Split off over one number: block size. Bigger blocks, cheaper payments, more centralization risk. Ethereum Bet that programmable state was worth giving up Bitcoin's minimalism. Solana-style chains Bet that consumer-app speed was worth trading away low node requirements. Monero and Zcash Bet that privacy was worth the heavier cryptography and the regulatory scrutiny that follows it. Stablecoins Bet that a dollar claim backed by an issuer or a collateral pool beats trusting a central bank's monetary policy. Kaspa Kept PoW and UTXO but replaced the single chain with a blockDAG, betting that ordering parallel blocks beats discarding them. Kaspa origin Kaspa's launch belongs in the history map Kaspa's fair launch wasn't the plan from day one. It's what was left after research, a company called DAGLabs, an April 2021 testnet, and several hardware, presale, and business-model paths all failed to become the launch structure. The origin page has the sourced version. Read Kaspa origin story Next step Use history to read current coins Every coin below inherited one of these design branches. The coin atlas shows which one. pages.title: Kaspa Origin Story: Fair Launch, Failed Plans, and Crescendo | Kaspa Explained
pages.h1: Kaspa's fair launch was the path left after the other paths failed
pages.description: A sourced Kaspa origin story: DAGLabs, PHANTOM/GHOSTDAG research, the April 2021 testnet, fair launch, early bugs, the Rust rewrite, Crescendo, and the Toccata boundary.
pages.text: Origin story Kaspa's fair launch was the path left after the other paths failed Kaspa's launch structure was not chosen. It was what remained after research into faster proof-of-work ordering ran through DAGLabs, an April 2021 testnet, and a hardware plan, a presale, and a DeFi-infrastructure pitch that each collapsed in turn. Summary: Kaspa grew from PHANTOM/GHOSTDAG research into a fair-launched Proof-of-Work blockDAG. Mainnet launched in November 2021 with no premine, insider allocation, or pre-sales; Crescendo later made 10 BPS live; Toccata is gated by DAA score 474,165,565. Launch thesis The origin story is a constraint story Research, startup funding, hardware plans, DeFi-sequencing ambitions, and community pressure collided for four years before the remaining path narrowed to one option: publish the network and let anyone mine. Every earlier structure would have made Kaspa answer to something outside the protocol: a hardware distribution deal, a presale contract, a startup balance sheet, or a supporting role inside someone else's app ecosystem. The fair launch proved nothing about future adoption, price, or technical success. What it did was remove the premine, the pre-sale, and the insider-allocation table from the starting line. Research first The problem came before the coin Bitcoin at high block rates has one weak point: two honest miners can solve a block seconds apart, and the single-chain rule throws one of those blocks' work away. Kaspa's research lineage starts from that exact waste. A blockDAG keeps both blocks visible instead of discarding one, then uses a rule like GHOSTDAG to order the resulting graph into one shared payment history. DBLP lists Yonatan Sompolinsky and Aviv Zohar's 2018 paper, PHANTOM: A Scalable BlockDAG Protocol , as an IACR ePrint publication. Kaspa.org traces Kaspa's lineage through the same blockDAG research line: SPECTRE, then PHANTOM, then the protocols running Kaspa today. Earlier interviews sharpen the through-line. A 2017 Epicenter episode presents GHOST and SPECTRE as attempts to scale Bitcoin-style Proof of Work with DAG structure instead of wasted parallel blocks. A 2018 Rethink Trust interview frames the same work around Layer One throughput, faster confirmation, and trustless base-layer design. DAGLabs and testnet The startup path existed before the fair launch Public sources disagree on when DAGLabs was founded. An April 26, 2021 Investing.com launch article says 2017, by Yonatan Sompolinsky and Guy Corem, with $8 million raised from Polychain and Accomplice. The HackerNoon interview intro says Sompolinsky founded DAGLabs in 2018 to commercialize DAG protocols. Both sources are public; they don't agree. The claim that holds up either way: DAGLabs funded and organized part of the pre-mainnet path before Kaspa became a public, community-mined network. Polychain belongs in the pre-mainnet DAGLabs funding story, and the framing cuts both ways. Kaspa had no token premine, insider allocation, or pre-sale. It also had a VC-funded DAGLabs prehistory that shaped the hardware, mining, and fair-launch debate before mainnet existed. Guy Corem's April 13, 2021 testnet note calls Kaspa a Golang implementation of Phantom/GHOSTDAG and a generalization of Nakamoto Consensus. The April 2021 Investing.com article lists the testnet bundle: full node, web wallet, faucet, Katnip block explorer, graph inspector, Kashboard. It framed the project as testnet first, mainnet later, with no pre-mining or founder allocations planned. On the code itself, use the source-backed version. Yonatan's Hashdag archive describes the original Kaspad codebase as an adaptation of the Bitcoin client btcd , written in Golang. That holds up; the unsourced "Bitcoin Core 0.19" claim floating around does not. Could-have-been paths The failed plans are part of the story ASIC and presale path Hashdag's 2020 community-launch archive said Kaspa would have no premine or founder rewards, and in the same breath described DAGLabs as a for-profit miner running a pre-launch ASIC-customization path and a DeFi-contract auction for rights to future Kaspa coins. Yonatan later said the hardware and ASIC-presale path never materialized: the optical ASIC hardware it depended on wasn't ready. DeFi sequencing path The April 2021 launch article framed Kaspa as faster ordering infrastructure for DeFi applications running on Ethereum. The later Uphold interview recap keeps the same theme underneath: Kaspa's specialization is sequencing, which matters most where transaction order and MEV move real money. That's the source for the "base sequencing layer for another ecosystem" idea. It is not a claim that Kaspa ever shipped as an Ethereum L2. Gamenet path Yonatan later called the gamenet attempt flawed: closer to a testnet with incentives bolted on than an actual mainnet. The launch design kept changing under pressure before the public network found the shape it has now. Fair-launch path In the HackerNoon interview, Yonatan called DAGLabs a failed attempt to reconcile venture-backed and fair-launch models. Investors pushed for launch despite no business model or ROI plan. Asked directly if Polychain pushed him to launch, he agreed that was one way to describe it, and added that Gadi pushed too, because he saw the potential. Launch The public network launched without a premine Kaspa.org's current lore page puts mainnet launch in November 2021: a fair-launched Proof-of-Work network with no premine, insider allocation, or pre-sales. The homepage adds the genesis-proof framing: every coin traces cryptographically back to an empty genesis. Mining created the entire supply; no allocation table set coins aside for insiders. The claim stays narrow on purpose. No premine means no official token allocation before mining started. It does not mean equal access to early mining. Yonatan later estimated Kaspa's core developers mined about 2.5% of total supply after launch. The Kaspa Wiki prehistory page puts the related DAGLabs/Polychain estimate below 3%, roughly 840 million KAS, and says the tighter number is probably closer to 2.5% and under 850 million KAS. That's early-miner context, a separate question from whether there was a premine. The 2025 Bitcoin Takeover interview adds firsthand texture: Yonatan described the launch as messy and reluctant, the gamenet idea overtaken by miners who simply kept mining. The two-week halt, in his account, was a recovery path that preserved the UTXO set through a second genesis pointing back to the last valid state. Early stress The chain had to survive real failure On November 23, 2021, Yonatan published "Kaspa (Black Tuesday)" after a network crash in the prior 48 hours. His account: the developers were not rolling back to an earlier preferred state, they were rebuilding and comparing a certainly-valid UTXO commitment after a memory problem. That's the sourced version of what circulates as the "two-week bug" story. A second stress test came later. Kaspalytics recorded a September 2023 dust attack where the UTXO count jumped from about 8 million to 62 million, a separate event from the November 2021 launch bug, not a sequel to it. Rust and Crescendo The original implementation was not the final form Hashdag's 2022 "Kaspa where to" archive says Michael Sutton proposed a major refactor and Rust rewrite because the Golang codebase carried technical debt that made it hard for new contributors to work in. Kaspa.org now summarizes that as a full rewrite from the original Golang node into Rust, funded by a community grant. Rusty Kaspa's repository describes the Rust implementation as a drop-in replacement for the older Golang node. Its README puts the Crescendo hard fork on May 5, 2025, moving the network from 1 BPS to 10 BPS. The v1.0.0 release notes name the exact trigger: mainnet DAA score 110,165,000. Toccata boundary Crescendo is live. Toccata activated separately "Toccata" gets misapplied to 10 BPS. It shouldn't be. Crescendo is the hard fork that made 10 BPS live on mainnet. Toccata is a separate, later hard fork: base-layer programmability with covenants, Silverscript, ZK-facing verification work, sequencing commitments, and native-asset groundwork, activated at DAA score 474,165,565. Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 is the current Toccata release; v2.0.0 shipped the activation. Wallet support, indexer support, and real app usage on top of Toccata are still building: check Toccata Status for where each of those stands. What to say The careful version holds up better Topic Use Avoid Code origin Original Kaspad was Golang and source-backed as an adaptation of btcd . Bitcoin Core 0.19, unless a durable source is added. DAGLabs DAGLabs funded and organized pre-mainnet work; public sources differ on 2017 versus 2018 dating. A single exact founding date with no caveat. Polychain Polychain belongs in the VC-funded DAGLabs prehistory. Premine and pre-sale allocation claims need separate token-allocation evidence. Ignoring Polychain context or treating it as proof of a premine. Fair launch No premine, insider allocation, or pre-sales; every coin came from mining, including the post-launch DAGLabs/Polychain-related early mining estimate. DAGLabs/Polychain premine language, flawless distribution, or no early contributor mining. Business failure Hardware, presale, and startup paths failed to materialize before the vanilla fair launch. Bankruptcy language unless a stronger source says bankruptcy. Toccata Base protocol activated on mainnet at DAA score 474,165,565 (Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1); wallet, indexer, and app support are separate, still-building claims. Toccata made Kaspa 10 BPS. Sources Sources for this origin page Kaspa.org Lore - current public summary for fair launch, research lineage, Rust rewrite, Crescendo, Toccata, DAGKnight, and roadmap framing. Kaspa.org homepage - genesis-proof framing for no premine, no hidden allocation, and fair launch. Polychain Capital homepage - Polychain's own high-level description as an investment firm for blockchain assets. pages.description: Kaspa in one screen: what works now, what comes next, where the edges are, and what would strengthen the thesis.
pages.text: Kaspa in one screen Kaspa keeps mined money and UTXO ownership, then changes the shape of the ledger. Instead of forcing every honest block into one slow line, it uses a blockDAG and GHOSTDAG so parallel honest work stays in the record and still gets ordered. Live today: Proof of Work, UTXO ownership, GHOSTDAG, the blockDAG, and the Crescendo-era 10 BPS network. Wallets, explorers, nodes, mining, transfers, receipts, and accepted-transaction checks all work now. Toccata activated at DAA 474,165,565. vProgs, native DeFi, and DAGKnight still need their own evidence. The May 2026 TN10 activation and hardening tests are testnet evidence, not mainnet. Summary Kaspa is a mined UTXO network betting that Proof-of-Work payments can feel closer to real time. The claim: Bitcoin-style mining can support lower-latency usage without turning into a normal centralized fast database. Live: PoW mining, UTXO ownership, blockDAG structure, GHOSTDAG ordering, 10 BPS mainnet, wallets, explorers, nodes, mining, transfers, receipts, and accepted-transaction checks. Still open: full vProgs, DAGKnight, native DeFi, TangVM/oracle systems, mature Toccata-era apps, and full app-to-app atomic composition. One-line read Bitcoin-style mining culture, seconds-scale user feel, blockDAG ordering, verifiable receipts today, and future apps that prove their own rules. Transaction payloads and accepted-transaction checks are live L1 evidence today. Toccata-era app rules, native assets, and vProgs each still need their own receipts, wallet support, explorer support, and product evidence. Suggested wording Use Avoid Kaspa is a live PoW blockDAG using GHOSTDAG. Kaspa has already shipped every roadmap item. Kaspa improves PoW inclusion and confirmation dynamics. Kaspa removes all finality delay or has unlimited throughput. Kaspa has a future roadmap for apps that prove rules and share ordering. Native DeFi and mature smart contracts are live today. 10 BPS is live, while TPS depends on measurement context. Every big testnet or lab number is normal mainnet throughput. Real-time means fast mined user feel with confirmation risk. Real-time means instant finality. Next checks What would strengthen the thesis: durable users, healthy mining, realistic node operation, liquidity, fees, wallets, developer tools, post-Toccata apps people actually keep using, and careful roadmap execution. What would weaken it: overclaiming roadmap work, weak adoption, poor liquidity, mining or infrastructure concentration, and app-layer promises that outrun shipped software. This page started as a May snapshot and picked up a June 29 pass on top: mainnet numbers, what moved in the Toccata release record, and where the wording in older Kaspa claims was too loose. Last checked: June 30, 2026. Re-run this check at emission step-downs, after new release or KIP activity, or when app and tooling evidence changes. KIP alignment The June 29 raw KIP check lists KIP-16 and KIP-20 as proposed and implemented, active on TN10; KIP-17 and KIP-21 as implemented and active on TN10. That's testnet and design evidence; mainnet activation is checked separately. Open KIP PRs KIP-24 adds transaction-v1 fields for compute budgets, covenant bindings, user lanes, and ZK-friendly txids. KIP-22 proposes P2MR ScriptPublicKey work for quantum resistance and MAST-style scripts. Both are still open pull requests, not merged code. TN10 activation tests Rusty Kaspa's tn10-toc2 pre-release set a Testnet-10 activation point at DAA score 467,579,632; tn10-toc3 set final Toccata ZK hardening at DAA 476,232,000. A June 29 Testnet-10 REST check showed virtual DAA 503,616,667: testnet evidence, not a mainnet claim. Argent Michael Sutton's Argent repo is early actor-style Silverscript tooling. It's prototype research: not audited, not stable, not evidence of mainnet activation. Builder tooling Python SDK v2.0.0 and v2.0.1 added Toccata-aligned wallet, lane-proof, SMT-sync, and covenant-binding support. Rusty Kaspa's merged ZK SDK PR adds an R0ScriptBuilder helper for RISC Zero proof scripts. Emission check The published schedule: 27.5 KAS/sec from May 8, 25.9565436 from June 7, 24.49971475 from July 7. It's a step-down, not a cliff: the schedule has no drop-off point. pages.title: Kaspa Risks and Open Questions | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: Kaspa risks and open questions: node pressure, security budget, Proof-of-Work external cost, liquidity, mining concentration, and app-roadmap execution risk.
pages.text: Risks Kaspa risks and open questions Five separate claims hold up the Kaspa case: fast PoW works as advertised, node operation stays independent at higher block rates, mining stays distributed, liquidity gets deep enough to matter, and Toccata's activated app-layer rules attract apps people actually use. Each one can fail without the others failing. Summary: nothing below is a hunch. Each objection names the mechanism that would break the case and the evidence that would settle it. Main objections Verification cost Higher block rates raise the bandwidth, CPU, and storage a node needs to keep up. Push that too far and independent verification concentrates in a handful of well-funded operators. Security budget Block rewards decline over time. Unless fees and demand replace that revenue, miner income falls and so does the cost of attacking the network. External cost PoW security is bought with electricity, ASICs, facilities, and supply chains. That cost is real and it does not disappear because the chain is fast. Liquidity Depth, custody, exchange support, and market-maker coverage do not follow automatically from good architecture. They take years and capital to build. Mining concentration ASIC supply is controlled by a small number of manufacturers. Pool concentration and geographic clustering can put practical control in few hands even with an open protocol. Roadmap execution Toccata activated on mainnet; vProgs, DAGKnight, and native DeFi are still separate engineering tracks on separate timelines. Treating them as one shipped bundle overstates how much is actually done. User demand Low fees and spare capacity are necessary for apps to exist. They are not evidence that anyone will use them twice. Good-faith concerns Faster blocks mean more data to propagate, validate, and store. Every node, indexer, wallet, explorer, and archival service absorbs that cost. The open question is whether that cost stays low enough for someone without a data-center budget to run a full node years from now, or whether it quietly becomes a service only a few providers can afford to offer. Security budget is arithmetic, not sentiment. As block rewards taper, miners need fees or token value to replace that revenue, or hash power leaves and the cost of a 51% attack drops with it. A high-throughput Proof-of-Work network still has to pay for its own security every block. Architecture does not buy liquidity. Ethereum, Solana, and Bitcoin got their market-maker depth, custody relationships, and developer mindshare through years of capital and usage, not through better consensus design. Kaspa has to build that the same slow way; a faster blockDAG does not shortcut it. Proof of Work's decentralization claim rests on mining distribution and pool behavior, not just on the algorithm. If a handful of pools or manufacturers control most hash power, the protocol can be open while practical control is not. The same risk exists one layer up: if most users reach the network through one explorer, one API provider, or one hosted wallet, that becomes the real chokepoint regardless of what the base layer allows. Proof-of-Work external cost Proof of Work prices Sybil resistance in physical goods: electricity, ASICs, facilities, cooling, supply chains, operators, geography, time. A miner cannot fake identities to gain influence: adding influence means adding hashpower, and hashpower costs money every hour it runs. That reshapes attack economics. An attacker needs hardware, energy contracts, and sustained operating cost, not just capital sitting in a wallet. New KAS enters circulation as a reward to miners who already spent those resources, a different issuance model from staking, where new supply and voting weight both trace back to existing token ownership. Sovereignty in a PoW system is not the same as sovereignty in a staking system. A node verifies the chain regardless of who mines it. Mining to your own node lets you help produce blocks, but you're still exposed to the same outside-world risks as every other miner: ASIC supply concentration, cheap-energy access, pool behavior, and regulation. PoW buys security with real-world cost, and real-world cost has real-world chokepoints. Evidence that would answer them Concern Weak answer Strong answer Node pressure Fast blocks sound good. Independent operators can run nodes, APIs, explorers, and indexers without relying on one provider. Security budget Price or enthusiasm will solve it. Fees, demand, value, and mining economics keep enough hash power securing the network over time. App roadmap A talk, branch, or testnet demo exists. Mainnet release, activation evidence, wallet support, indexer support, accepted transactions, and repeatable user flows exist. Liquidity There are holders and volume. Users can enter, exit, custody, account for funds, get support, and trade with meaningful depth. Demand Low fees make apps possible. People use apps repeatedly because the app solves a job better with Kaspa than with a normal server. App ambition can outrun evidence Toccata, based apps, ZK verification, future vProgs, native DeFi, coordination markets, and DAGKnight are separate engineering tracks moving at separate speeds. A testnet demo of one is not mainnet evidence for the rest, and it is not mainnet evidence for the one it demoed, either. Risk What would answer it? Toccata tooling stays rough after activation. Toccata activated at DAA score 474,165,565 on Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1. What's left to verify: stable releases, working docs, and repeatable builder examples. TN10/TN12 tests alone are not enough. Native apps remain demos without usage. Repeat users, fee demand, repeatable apps, wallet support, and independent indexers. DeFi claims get ahead of custody and oracle reality. Audited custody rules, real wallet signing, oracle design, liquidation rules, and accepted settlement evidence. Based-app language becomes too abstract. Concrete products where app state is anchored to Kaspa ordering, proofs, settlement, or exits. What to watch Count the number of independent explorers, APIs, wallets, and node operators. More of them means less dependence on any single interface going down or going bad. Watch whether roadmap items turn into applications with repeat users outside the teams that built them, not just working demos. Liquidity, custody support, and fee demand will decide whether the thesis holds regardless of how the architecture performs. And watch the language: during a hype cycle, live, testnet, roadmap, and research claims get flattened into one story first. For the price and hash-rate version of this risk, read Kaspa price, hash rate, and the mining cycle . Read the May 2026 status check , open the claims checker , or open the source guide .
