pages.title: Kaspa vProgs Explained: Resource Lanes, Proofs, and App Composition | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: How Kaspa vProgs schedule app state by resource, prove execution with ZK, and where Toccata's covenants stop short of native DeFi.
pages.text: Roadmap architecture Kaspa vProgs explained Two vProgs transactions touching different resources never wait on each other, no matter how busy the network is. That's the whole scheduling trick: name every piece of app state as a resource, let a transaction declare which ones it reads and writes, run the ones that don't collide in parallel, and prove the result to Kaspa L1 instead of replaying every step on it. Status: vProgs are prototype and roadmap work. Toccata is the activated L1 expressiveness surface. Full vProgs and native Kaspa DeFi are not live on mainnet. Builder guide Application layer Toccata status One sentence The mental model Work that touches the same resource waits in line. Work that doesn't, never sees the line. Resource A coin, balance, object, order, vault, game position, or app-specific state item, named so the scheduler can track it. Dependency A transaction declares which resources it reads and writes. That declaration is what lets the scheduler decide what can run together. Proof The app produces proofs or journals so later layers can verify what happened without re-executing every step on L1. Scheduling Why resource lanes exist A global account model makes every app action compete for the same shared state, even when the actions have nothing to do with each other. vProgs break that state apart into individually addressable resources instead. Alice touching resource A and Bob touching resource Z run at the same time, no queue between them. Two transactions touching the same resource A still have to settle their order, so the scheduler serializes only that piece. The scheduler builds this from the read/write metadata a transaction declares up front. Each resource behaves like its own lane: a transaction attaches to the lanes it touches, waits only for the values it needs, runs the moment those are ready, then passes its updated state forward. The result is a computational DAG, not a single queue. Independent branches keep executing while a busy resource only slows the transactions that actually collide with it. Hans Moog's vProgs walkthrough does not claim a raw TPS number. The claim is narrower and more useful: app state that doesn't conflict keeps moving even while one resource or market is under load. Layer map What the prototype repo shows The public kaspanet/vprogs repository calls itself an early-development Rust framework for based computation on Kaspa. Its README splits the framework into six layers: core types, storage, state, scheduling, transaction runtime, and node integration, plus separate L1 and ZK crates for bridge/types, ABI, transaction prover, batch prover, VM, and a RISC Zero backend. Layer Job Why it exists Core Shared types for resources, transactions, and access metadata. Every other layer reads and writes the same basic types. Storage Reads and writes app state to disk. Persistence without storage code knowing app semantics. State Defines what gets stored and how versions or rollbacks work. Execution needs a fixed model for resource state. Scheduling Tracks resource access and orchestrates parallel execution. Independent resource lanes run without one global lock. Runtime Defines what a transaction or program does when it executes. Different VMs or app runtimes plug into the same scheduling model. Node Assembles the layers into a runnable system. A framework on paper still needs one integrated binary. ZK / L1 Produces proofs and ties app results back to Kaspa evidence. Verification and settlement have to land somewhere concrete. Toccata connection What comes before full vProgs Toccata is the hard-fork track that shipped before any of this: activated, not upcoming. Its release and KIP work delivered covenant-style spending rules, covenant IDs, ZK proof checks, and sequencing commitments, concrete handles for UTXO state constraints, app-state identity, selected computation proofs, and app-local sequencing anchored to Kaspa evidence. Michael Sutton's Argent repo is early tooling evidence, not a finished product: actor-style state machines that generate Silverscript for multi-contract covenant systems. It's prototype work worth studying. Audit, production, and activation are separate claims that need separate evidence. None of that makes full vProgs live. Toccata can carry simpler covenant apps, proof-gated flows, sequencing commitments, and standalone based-app foundations. Full app-to-app composition, one action touching several app states that succeeds or fails as a unit, is the later target. Near-term Covenants, spend constraints, asset rules, proof checks, lane-friendly commitments. Based app One app anchors its state to Kaspa ordering: commitments, proofs, settlement, exits. Full vProgs Later architecture for richer logic and cross-app atomic composition. Copy boundary Claim wording Use Avoid Reason vProgs are roadmap architecture for app programs that prove richer logic while sharing Kaspa ordering. Treating vProgs as activated Kaspa smart contracts. The public repo is prototype code. Mainnet activation needs its own mainnet evidence. Toccata gives Kaspa a path to L1 app rules and based-app foundations. Toccata means full Kaspa DeFi is live. Activation, wallets, liquidity, audits, custody, and app usage are each separate evidence. Independent resource lanes execute without waiting on unrelated congested state. Kaspa apps have unlimited throughput. Parallelism depends on workload shape and which resources a transaction declares. ZK proves a statement about chosen public inputs. A proof automatically proves prices, bridge truth, or real-world events. External facts need an anchor: a light client, oracle, reporter set, or challenge process. Builder filter When this architecture applies The vProgs model fits products with many independent pieces of state, many users hitting the same app, or a proof requirement bigger than a covenant spend can carry: trading state, auctions, games, coordination markets, app-specific ledgers, proof-backed settlement. Most Kaspa apps do not need it yet. Payments, receipts, vault rules, refund paths, allowance caps, and controlled assets fit inside covenants today. Pick the smallest state model that does the job honestly, and reach for vProgs only when the app actually outgrows it. pages.title: Kaspa TPS Explained: Payments, Toccata, ZK Apps, and vProgs | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: Kaspa TPS is not one number. Simple L1 payments run 2.5k-3.4k TPS at 10 BPS. Covenant transactions, ZK settlements, and vProg throughput each need their own math.
pages.text: Capacity question Kaspa TPS, explained by workload A single Kaspa TPS number does not exist. Simple L1 payments sit in one range. Covenant apps, ZK settlements, token rules, and future vProg-style systems each run their own math against a different bottleneck. Status checked June 30, 2026: Kaspa mainnet runs the Crescendo-era 10 BPS network. Toccata activated at DAA 474,165,565 and changed proof and covenant capacity. Ordinary payment TPS tracks the 10 BPS network and transaction mix. Current status Toccata status vProgs Implementation links Direct answer Ask "TPS of what?" Workload Answer Why the number changes Simple L1 payments Roughly 2.5k to 3.4k TPS for ordinary simple transfers. Set by 10 BPS and block-mass limits against simple transaction mass. Other workloads need their own assumptions. Covenant or programmable L1 transactions Workload-specific, often below simple-payment TPS. Covenants add script work, state constraints, covenant identifiers, output rules, inputs, outputs, fees, and storage effects. ZK proof or settlement transactions Fewer, heavier L1 transactions. One proof or settlement transaction can carry many off-chain app actions. Bounded by proof system, proof size, verification cost, batch size, proving time, and settlement design. Effective ZK app or future vProg throughput App-specific, and can exceed raw L1 transaction TPS for a given design. The metric is app actions per proof batch or settlement cycle, with state access and prover work as the real limits. Simple payments Current simple-payment capacity Kaspa mainnet produces ten blocks per second. The shared block mass limit in current mainnet parameters is 500,000, which sets a budget of 5,000,000 transaction mass per second before policy, fees, propagation, storage shape, and real mempool behavior enter the picture. A signed ordinary P2PK-style 1-input, 1-output payment costs roughly 1.6k mass in conservative code-based arithmetic. Add a change output and a 1-input, 2-output payment runs closer to 2.0k mass. Divide the block budget by those shapes and the count lands around 250 to 300 simple transactions per block: the mid-2k to low-3k TPS lane at 10 BPS. Leaner shapes and rounding push the upper end to the commonly cited 3.4k TPS. Use roughly 2.5k to 3.4k TPS for current simple payments, and name the assumption behind it: transaction shape times block mass. Artificial minimum-transaction ceilings can score higher, but they measure a lab envelope, not ordinary payment throughput. Mental model About 250 to 300 simple payment transactions per block at 10 BPS. Boundary That model covers simple payments only. It does not describe covenant apps, proof settlements, or token state machines. What to specify Transaction shape, inputs, outputs, scripts, payload, fee policy, and whether the number is capacity, demand, or a lab result. Mass model Simple tx/block stops at payments A raw count of transactions per block hides Kaspa's real limit: mass, not envelope count. The implementation charges for serialized bytes, script-public-key bytes, signature-operation or compute-budget work, transient byte mass, and storage mass effects. A larger transaction eats a larger slice of the block budget regardless of how the mempool counts it. App transactions change the footprint. More inputs, more outputs, larger scripts, covenant metadata, payload data, proof bytes, or state-transition evidence all crowd out simple transfers competing for the same mass budget. Node-side repeated work moves the ceiling further: validation cost, propagation size, UTXO access patterns, storage effects, and app-specific indexing. Payload data has its own bound. Kaspa's docs put the payload ceiling around 25 KB when payload data dominates a standard transaction, because the standard transaction mass ceiling and transient byte accounting still apply on top of it. App data spends the same block capacity payments spend. Toccata What Toccata changes Toccata doubles the transient mass budget without touching the payment-relevant limit. It is mainly a programmability upgrade: it changes what Kaspa L1 transactions can express and verify, covenant-style spending rules, covenant IDs, ZK verifier infrastructure, sequencing-commitment access, and the first base-layer foundations for based-ZK apps. A TPS number still needs to name its workload. The Toccata guide and current params show one throughput-relevant change: transient mass rises from 500,000 to 1,000,000 at activation, while the compute and storage reference limit holds at 500,000. The guide frames the increase around fitting STARK-sized proofs, not around raising payment throughput. Toccata also adds v1 transaction fields such as output covenant data and input compute commitments, and raises the standard minimum relay fee. Piece What it adds TPS implication KIP-17 covenants Transaction introspection, byte operations, hashing tools, signature checks from stack, and script tools for stateful UTXO rules. More expressive transactions run heavier than simple payments. KIP-20 covenant IDs Stable covenant lineage through a 32-byte covenant identifier and authorizing input binding. Backs asset rules and state machines at the cost of extra metadata and validation work. KIP-16 ZK precompile OpZkPrecompile for proof verification paths such as Groth16 and RISC0-Succinct. Proof transactions spend L1 capacity on verification, not transfer count. KIP-21 sequencing commitments Partitioned lane commitments so app proving can track app activity instead of the entire DAG. Cuts app proving cost. It is not itself an end-user TPS number. Covenants and assets Programmable transactions consume capacity differently One token transfer in a wallet can cost several times the mass of a plain payment. A covenant transaction carries rules about how its coins or state can be spent next, which is what makes vaults, escrow, assurance contracts, controlled assets, and token-like rules possible. That structure costs more than a simple payment. The user sees one action. The L1 footprint depends on the asset rule underneath it: covenant state, covenant IDs, authorization rules, extra outputs, witness data, app payloads, or indexer-readable state. Counting that transaction as equivalent to an ordinary payment hides its real capacity cost. Simple-payment TPS is a payment metric. Covenant-app throughput needs its own count, built from the actual transaction shape and state pattern. ZK proofs ZK changes the metric One L1 transaction can settle thousands of off-chain actions. ZK proof systems move app execution off the base layer and keep a compact verification path on L1: a single proof or settlement transaction updates an app commitment after many off-chain actions run. The L1 transaction count stays small while the app action count grows large. That does not make TPS unlimited. Effective app throughput is bounded by the app, proof system, batch size, proof size, proving hardware, proof-generation time, data availability, settlement cadence, exit rules, and bridge/oracle assumptions. A ZK proof proves a statement about chosen inputs. External facts still need an anchor: a light client, finality certificate, accumulated-work view, reporter set, oracle, or challenge process. The metric that matters for a ZK app is app actions per settlement cycle, with L1 proof verification as the bottleneck. That number can run far above L1 transaction TPS for a single app, and it is still bounded by proof economics and state design. vProgs vProgs remain roadmap architecture Toccata ships the parts vProg-style systems need without shipping vProgs: covenants, proof checks, covenant IDs, and partitioned sequencing commitments. Full vProgs are a later architecture for app programs that prove richer logic while sharing Kaspa ordering. vProgs remain roadmap work, not a live system. KIP-21 stops every prover from having to follow the entire DAG for every app. Its partitioned commitment design targets O(activity) proving: a prover for one app lane follows that lane's activity, not total network activity. Current parameters cap user-lane churn at 50 non-coinbase lanes per block and 1,000,000,000 gas per lane. At 10 BPS, that is a worst-case bound of 500 user-lane updates per second. User transaction throughput still needs its own transaction-shape assumptions on top. The public kaspanet/vprogs repository shows the implementation direction: resource access, scheduling, batches, state diffs, transaction runtime, L1, and ZK components. Michael Sutton's Argent repo is related tooling research for composing multi-contract covenant apps into Silverscript. Neither repo is mainnet activation evidence for full vProgs. Checklist How to discuss Kaspa capacity Workload Name whether the number covers simple payments, covenant spends, token rules, proof settlements, or app actions. Transaction shape List inputs, outputs, scripts, payload, covenant fields, proof bytes, and storage effects. Block assumptions State BPS, block-mass limits, standardness limits, fee policy, and mainnet versus testnet context. App/proof design For ZK and vProg-style systems, state batch size, proving cost, settlement cadence, state access, and exit design. Roughly 2.5k to 3.4k TPS holds only for current simple L1 payment transfers. For Toccata apps, covenants, ZK proofs, tokens, and vProgs, the first question is "TPS of what?" pages.text: Founder analysis Kaspa fintech for founders Kaspa fits a fintech product when the design specifically needs self-custodied value, fast payment visibility, or public evidence that survives even if the operator running the app disappears. Status: payments are live today. Toccata activated at DAA score 474,165,565 on Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1. Wallet support, tooling, and app receipts for the new rule surface are still catching up. Where a public network changes the product Payment receipts Invoices, settlement records, refunds, and support flows can show txid, amount, address, accepted status, source, and timestamp. Treasury controls Teams use spending limits, delayed withdrawals, recovery paths, or approvals that users can inspect before funds move. Escrow and refunds A buyer, seller, or sponsor can rely on visible release, refund, timeout, or cancel paths through Toccata's activated covenant rules, once wallet and tooling support catch up. Proof-backed workflow The app publishes a receipt or state row that another wallet, support desk, or auditor can check independently. Where Kaspa is a poor fit A normal fintech database wins when the product needs chargebacks, private ledgers, fast customer-service reversals, fiat-only payments, or one regulated operator with final say over every state change. Kaspa earns its place in the design only when users actually need self-custody, public ordering, neutral settlement, or rules that stay visible even after the app's operator changes. pages.title: Kaspa Covenants Explained: Spend Rules for UTXO Apps | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: How Kaspa covenants restrict a UTXO's next spend: vaults, escrow, controlled assets, and assurance contracts, with Toccata status on each.
pages.text: Builder intake Kaspa covenants explained A Kaspa covenant restricts how a coin can be spent next, not just who can spend it. A budget that can't be drained in one transaction, a vault with a separate recovery path, an asset that requires an issuer's signature to move: each is the same primitive applied to a different rule. Status: payments are live today. Toccata's app-layer rules still need wallet support, tooling support, and app receipts before builders can ship on them. How covenants work A normal signature answers one question: is this spender authorized? A covenant answers a second one: does the next output preserve the rule? Consensus inspects the spending transaction itself and can require the following output to route funds a certain way, cap the value that moves, or carry state forward into the next UTXO. That turns a piece of app logic into a rule the chain enforces directly, one a user can check without trusting an operator. It does not remove wallet UX work, audits, liquidity, legal exposure, or oracle design. Those stay separate problems. Covenant IDs prove lineage A covenant constrains how one UTXO moves next. On its own, that's not enough to stop someone from forging a lookalike UTXO with similar-looking rules but no real history. A covenant ID closes that gap: consensus tags a UTXO as belonging to a specific covenant family, so a fake with copied logic still fails the lineage check. Piece Plain job Consequence Normal script Checks who is allowed to spend. Handles ownership and ordinary payments. Covenant Checks whether the next output preserves a rule. Builds vaults, escrow paths, controlled assets, and state transitions. Covenant ID Tags a UTXO's covenant family across valid continuations. Stops lookalike forgeries and makes membership indexable. For the broader upgrade frame, read Toccata Explained . Primary reference: KIP-20 covenant IDs . Examples Budget that can't be drained at once A treasury output requires each next spend to leave a minimum balance or stay under a cap, so no single transaction empties it. Withdrawal with recovery A vault splits normal withdrawal and emergency recovery into separate paths, each with its own conditions. Asset with controller A ticket or pass requires an issuer or controller signature on the input before it can transfer or redeem. Commitment with refund A funding rule releases only after a value threshold is met, and refunds automatically if the threshold is missed. Covenant evidence checklist User need. Name what the user is doing before naming the opcode or compiler. Accepted path. Point to the accepted transaction or test artifact. Rejected path. Show what fails when the rule is violated. Status label. Live, testnet, targeted, roadmap, or research. Missing product work. Wallet signing, audits, indexing, support, liquidity, and custody gaps that still need filling. That's why most apps ship there first. Live territory today is payments, receipts, node reads, and API work. Covenant-style app rules are activated at the protocol level but thin on wallet and tooling support. Need PoW settlement feel? pages.text: Reality check Test the pitch before the narrative A protocol activating on schedule doesn't tell you whether an app built on top of it actually works. Product claims need a different test: who uses it, what they do, where the liquidity comes from, what the wallet flow looks like, and what evidence backs any of it up. Use this for app and product claims. For protocol status, use the claims checker . When a demo or txid is being used to prove a builder claim, use builder evidence . Test a pitch Use the checklist Keyword pre-check Paste a product idea A keyword scan for whether the pitch even touches the basic product questions a real review would ask. Next pass Copy the review prompt, then compare the pitch against Status, Claims, and Sources before posting. Copy review prompt Prompt updates as you type. Product reality The eight questions 01 Who is the user? Name the actor: trader, wallet user, merchant, miner, exchange, issuer, developer, fund, or app operator. "Everyone" isn't an answer. 02 What job do they do? Send, swap, borrow, hedge, launch, redeem, escrow, stake, report, integrate, verify. "Platform" is a word that hides the job. 03 Where is liquidity? Name the first market: issuer, LP, market maker, stablecoin, treasury, buyers, or earned revenue. "Community" doesn't source a market. 04 Who signs what? Trace the wallet flow, the transaction shape, the custody model, the recovery path, and what the user sees when it fails. 05 What exists today? Live mainnet, app tooling, testnet proof, a targeted upgrade, roadmap, or research: five different answers, not one. 06 What evidence proves it? A source link, an accepted transaction, code, docs, an audit, release notes, a working app path, or a command someone else can run. 07 What breaks? Model abuse, oracle failure, a liquidity exit, wallet mistakes, insider allocation, bot traffic, downtime, legal or custody risk. 08 What happens on day two? Real products keep showing up after launch: retention, support, integrations, revenue, routes, or usage someone can measure. Real versus fake Signals to separate Claim type Real signal Weak signal Kaspa question Launchpad Issuance, wallet flow, a liquidity path, visible holders, abuse controls. A token button and a roadmap. What can launch today, and where does the liquidity actually come from? Is this live mainnet, TN10/TN12 testnet evidence, or just an app idea riding on Toccata's name? AI agent The agent signs, pays, receives, proves work, or triggers a bounded workflow on-chain. Chatbot copy wrapped around a token. What action actually happens on Kaspa, and who can verify it? Wallet Clear signing, recovery, balances, history, error states, source verification. Nice screens with no real transaction handling underneath. Does a normal user know what they're signing? Institutional use Custody, compliance, reporting, settlement, liquidity, support, integration requirements. One vague partnership post. Which institution, which requirement, and what's the evidence? pages.title: Kaspa Builder Guide | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: A builder guide for choosing the simplest Kaspa route: money movement, covenant spend rules, based apps, inline ZK, or later app programs.
pages.text: Kaspa builder guide Architecture is the wrong starting point. Start with the user action: a payment, a vault rule, an asset rule, a market, a proof, or a later app-to-app flow. Only ask about state once that action is specific. Default: start with the smallest working path. Mainnet status comes from activation, releases, and working applications, not architecture diagrams. Need terminal commands first? Open Kaspa Command Line From Zero . 1 / Job Name the action Send, receive, lock, refund, issue, replay, prove, or settle: one verb, not a paragraph. 2 / Path Pick the smallest path Payment path, app receipt, covenant rule, based app, proof, or later app program: pick the cheapest one that still does the job. 3 / Evidence Show what landed Accepted txid, app receipt, state output, replay row, source, or release record: something a stranger can check without asking you. 4 / Boundary Say what is missing Mainnet activation, wallet support, liquidity, audit, indexer, oracle, or production custody: name the actual gap, not "more work needed." Build around verifiable evidence A repeatable Kaspa example does four things in order: names the user action, submits or inspects a transaction, replays the result, and labels the evidence class before anyone makes a bigger claim on top of it. Good first example Payment or receipt A user sends tKAS or attaches app data; the page links the accepted txid and states exactly what changed. Good covenant example Rule that blocks a bad spend Put the cap, destination, required controller input, refund, or timeout in front of the reader before the artifact details. Weak example Mechanism without a user need Naming the internal mechanism before the user problem is the tell of a weak example. Start with state and proofs Question Use this path Simpler path Many users touch the same app state at the same time. Start with based apps or vProgs-compatible runtime work. Start with covenants and L1 state outputs instead. The product splits into independent states. Covenants still work, one per separate state. Shared-state app architecture fits better here. Each action needs its own proof, privacy check, or custom validity rule. Inline ZK is the fit, but it costs more proof and operations work than the alternatives. Covenants or based apps handle this more cheaply. The proof depends on another chain, an oracle, a price, or a real-world event. Name the anchor first: source root, finality certificate, accumulated-work view, oracle, reporter set, or challenge process, before writing any proof code. The proof stays inside the app's own state rules, no external anchor needed. The app needs synchronous composition with other independent apps. That's the future full-vProgs direction , especially once several app states must succeed or fail as one operation. Build the narrow app first. Toccata apps coordinate through L1 proofs and sequencing without full atomic composition. Match app model to state model Covenants handle constrained spend rules: vaults, treasury controls, escrow-like flows, unlock conditions, issuance policy, small UTXO state machines. One protected state advances one valid step at a time. That constraint is the entire mechanism. Based apps carry richer app state anchored to Kaspa ordering: balances, orders, packs, risk rows, task states, market state. Start with deterministic replay over accepted transactions. Add ZK only once proof-verified execution, privacy, or trust-minimized bridge logic becomes the actual product boundary, not before. Inline ZK covers actions that need their own proof before settlement. Full vProgs are the later app-to-app composition direction, where independent apps read or call one another in one combined outcome. Say what the example buys the user Every builder example needs a user job attached to the artifact: a budget that can't be drained at once, an asset that only moves under a controller rule, a game turn that can't get stuck forever, a payout that can be replayed, a group payment that refunds if the condition fails. Show artifacts in this order: what landed on TN12, what the reader can click or repeat, what the repo replayed from accepted rows, which rule is script-enforced versus replay-derived or wallet policy, and what's still missing before this becomes a real product claim. Keep the boundary honest past that point. Name the script path if the rule is script-enforced. Say so plainly if it's wallet policy, planner state, replay-derived state, or testnet-only evidence. The claim is strongest when the reader can see both the accepted path and the rejected path side by side. Run every covenant example through the same template: user need, spend rule, accepted path, rejected path, wallet review field, remaining blocker. Say "budget that cannot drain at once," "step-by-step workflow," or "asset that needs its controller" before naming the mechanism. For the public application framing, see what TN12 covenant tests are teaching . For the current testnet examples, open the TN12 experiment map . Map product ideas to a path Pick the smallest path that matches the product. Most first builds land on a wallet/payment path, a covenant-shaped rule, or a narrow based app, not the full stack. Open product-path table Product shape Likely starting path Why Vault, treasury, inheritance, recovery, escrow Covenants Who can move funds, and how the stateful output evolves, is the whole product. Nothing else needed. Native asset issuance or transfer policy Covenants Asset-native logic stays close to L1 output rules most of the time. Trading venue, game economy, shared balance app Based app Many users update the same app record at once, without waiting for one UTXO path to clear first. Private action, custom validity check, proof-gated workflow Inline ZK The proof rides along with every action, so verification is the product boundary, not a feature. Composable app network with calls across independent apps Full vProgs later App-to-app synchronous composition is the longer architecture target, not a current option. Builder tools SDK and node entry points live at Kaspa.org Build and the official getting-started docs . Toccata releases, KIPs, Silverscript, vProgs, ZK SDK, Python SDK, WASM docs, hosted APIs, indexers, and node infrastructure are tracked in Sources . Hosted APIs work fine for prototypes and dashboards. Products that sign transactions, track balances, handle custody, or promise uptime need a node, an indexer, a provider-redundancy plan, usually all three. Before prototyping Pick network first. Mainnet uses kaspa: . TN12 uses kaspatest: . Reusing test keys for mainnet is how funds get lost. Use the right node. Testnet covenant work needs a branch or release built for that testnet. Mainnet builders run the released mainnet node, not a testnet fork. Check sync and UTXO index. An unsynced local node or a missing index returns a balance that looks real and isn't. Separate UI policy from consensus rules. A mockup, planner state, or wallet warning is not an enforced covenant. The chain doesn't know the UI exists. Record exact submit details. Log SDK version, node version, network id, endpoint, encoding, tx version, and input budget fields every time, not just when something breaks. Prove the state change After submit, fetch accepted state and diff it against what the app claims happened. If they match, say so. If they don't, that's the bug report. Open verification checklist Builder habit Consequence Check Fetch accepted state after submit Local construction proves you built a transaction. It doesn't prove the network accepted it. Record `is_accepted`, accepting block data, output script type, address, and amount. Pin the submit surface REST, JSON wRPC, Borsh wRPC, SDK versions, and testnet branches can each hand back a different transaction shape for the same request. Log SDK version, node version, network id, endpoint, encoding, tx version, and input budget fields. Compare with a known working spend Witness order, signature preimage, redeem-script shape, and constructor keys are far easier to debug against a sibling transaction that already worked than in isolation. Diff the failing path against an accepted release, refund, or simple payment path before blaming protocol rules. Label failed attempts narrowly A tooling failure and a consensus failure look identical from the outside. They need different labels or the next builder repeats your mistake. Keep the artifact, but mark it as bad config, stale tooling, submit mismatch, or confirmed consensus rejection. Testnet lesson: the verification habit transfers, the prototype's status doesn't. One testnet demo is not a mainnet claim. Say the stage first Covenants: the L1 state-output path, live on mainnet, for constrained asset and UTXO-state rules. Based apps: app-specific state anchored to Kaspa ordering, commitments, proofs, settlement, or exits. Inline ZK: a specialized proof path for actions whose validity or privacy proof is the product boundary. External anchors: ZK checks a statement about chosen inputs. Builders still have to define how source-chain roots, prices, events, or attestations become trusted inputs. That part isn't automatic. Based-zk apps: based apps that add proof-verified execution or bridge logic once deterministic replay stops being enough. Full vProgs: the future app-to-app atomic composition direction, beyond standalone based-app construction. Transaction payloads: live L1 transaction data for receipts and app context today. Native smart-contract activation is a separate claim with its own evidence. State the stage plainly first. Add a caveat only where a reader could otherwise mistake builder work for live mainnet functionality. Build from current status Choose the model. Then verify current implementation state before writing docs or product claims, not after. Open status App ideas Builder references Izio's Kaspa programmability overview lays out the builder decision tree: covenants, based apps, inline ZK, future full vProgs. Izio on Covenants covers sequential protected-output state, covenant IDs, and the current Silverscript builder reference. Izio on Based Apps covers shared-state app architecture and Rust app logic in a managed environment. Izio on Inline ZK covers per-action proofs and proof-driven settlement. Izio on Full vProgs covers the future app-to-app synchronous composition direction. Rusty Kaspa tn10-toc3 pre-release , tn10-toc2 , and Testnet-10 REST status document the May 2026 Testnet-10 Toccata activation and hardening path. rusty-kaspa TN12 branch , Silverscript , and TN12 faucet cover testnet covenant prototyping. These are testnet builder tools, separate from mainnet activation evidence. Rusty Kaspa ZK SDK PR #953 merged the R0ScriptBuilder helper around RISC Zero proof scripts: tooling progress, not a claim about mature mainnet ZK apps. KIP-24 is the open transaction-v1 fields and hashing PR; KIP-22 is the open P2MR quantum-resistance ScriptPublicKey proposal. Both stay design/proposal evidence until merged and activated. Kaspa.org Build indexes current developer resources: Rusty Kaspa, WASM SDK, public node access, REST API, Docker, DB dumps, testnet, KIPs, Silverscript, vProgs, community infra, R&D links. Kaspa Developer Platform docs cover hosted address history, transaction acceptance, block-range, and node RPC proxy APIs. Hosted infrastructure doesn't set protocol status. That's a separate question. Kaspa docs , especially Getting started , Programmability , Transaction payload , Accepted transactions , and Kaspa node , cover current builder workflow. Aspectron RpcClient docs , signTransaction docs , and submit-transaction request docs define the JavaScript SDK request shape used in current builder examples. KasSigner and KasSee are experimental external-signer and watch-only wallet references: wallet UX and signing-boundary research, not shipped protocol status. Kaspa Explained status and source hierarchy hold the live/targeted/roadmap/research boundaries. Keep reading Next pages Previous Test the pitch before the narrative A Kaspa product-reality checklist and pitch scanner for testing crypto app claims against users, liquidity, wallet flows, evidence, and... Next What can you build on Kaspa now? Kaspa builder recipes: read DAG data, watch accepted transactions, track UTXOs, generate receipts, verify a txid, and replay TN12 evidence. Status Kaspa current status Kaspa status in plain buckets: live, targeted, roadmap, research, and claims that need caveats.

pages.title: What Can You Build on Kaspa Now? | Kaspa Explained
pages.h1: What can you build on Kaspa now?
pages.description: Kaspa builder recipes: read DAG data, watch accepted transactions, track UTXOs, generate receipts, verify a txid, and replay TN12 evidence.
pages.text: Build now What can you build on Kaspa now? Start where the chain answers back: network reads, accepted transactions, wallet flows, UTXOs, receipts, testnet practice. Toccata adds new rule surfaces on top, but it doesn't replace the need for receipts, tooling, wallets, and actual users. Summary: Kaspa builds today are payment, read, receipt, monitoring, API, UTXO, and verification tools. Toccata expands the app rule surface after activation. Recipes Small builds that work now Build Status First proof Read current DAG information Live Server info, block count, DAA score, or blue score: pull any of these from a node, a public node, or a documented API. Watch accepted transactions Live Listen or poll for accepted transaction IDs, then record the accepting block context alongside each one. Track address UTXOs Live Wallet software, your own node with a UTXO index, or a documented hosted API each cover a prototype. Generate a payment receipt page Live Amount, address, txid, accepted status, source, timestamp, fallback verification links: a receipt page needs all seven. Build wallet-confirmation UX Live Seen, included, ordered, accepted, and confidence-increasing are five distinct states, not one blur called "pending." Plan a data/indexer path Live The community API or public nodes cover prototypes. Production forces the decision on a dedicated node, indexer, archival data, or provider redundancy. Build payload-aware receipts Live Transaction payload docs plus accepted-transaction evidence plus an explicit source label lets the user verify the receipt's claim independently. Replay a TN12 covenant proof Testnet Record network, txid, accepted evidence, script path, and exactly what stays testnet-only. Infrastructure Pick the evidence path early Every app needs address history, accepted-transaction state, UTXO views, timestamps, pagination, and a fallback for the moment an API goes stale or drops offline. Prototype Documented hosted APIs, public nodes, explorers, and database dumps are fine for quick reads and demos. No infrastructure commitment needed yet. Production Running Rusty Kaspa, a UTXO index, a transaction indexer, archival storage, or redundant providers becomes a decision, not an option, once uptime matters. User trust Show the exact source behind each receipt or status check. Give a fallback path for the moment one API disagrees with another or simply times out. Builder loop Turn each build into a source-linked page Six things a reviewer needs before believing a Kaspa build claim. Input Name the exact user action: send, receive, watch, verify, issue, redeem, refund, or replay. Evidence Name the source: node, API, wallet, accepted transaction, code, release, or testnet proof. Status Live, testnet, targeted, roadmap, research, wrong, or unsupported: pick one. Failure mode Name the specific risk: stale API, unsynced node, wallet support, indexer mismatch, or activation gap. Share link Short enough to paste whole into Discord, Reddit, Telegram, X, docs, or a GitHub issue. Next source Point the reader to docs, command-line verification, status, and sources, not a dead end. Next Go deeper Verify a transaction Builder guide Toccata status Sources Keep reading Next pages Previous Kaspa builder guide A builder guide for choosing the simplest Kaspa route: money movement, covenant spend rules, based apps, inline ZK, or later app programs. Next How to verify a Kaspa transaction yourself How to verify a Kaspa transaction yourself: use explorers, second sources, wallets, hosted APIs, nodes, RPC, and accepted-transaction... pages.title: How to Verify a Kaspa Transaction Yourself | Kaspa Explained
pages.h1: How to verify a Kaspa transaction yourself
pages.description: How to verify a Kaspa transaction yourself: use explorers, second sources, wallets, hosted APIs, nodes, RPC, and accepted-transaction checks without trusting one interface.
pages.text: Verify yourself How to verify a Kaspa transaction yourself A wallet screen shows a balance and asks you to believe it. A node, an RPC call, or a second explorer either agrees or doesn't. This path moves from explorer output to a node, CLI, hosted API, or testnet check you can run yourself. Run a node Open CLI Hosted API checks Use testnet TN12 practice Sources Mainnet commands change with releases. Check the source links before touching real funds. Start here Pick the job Verify chain state Run or query a node, compare explorers side by side, and check whether a transaction is actually accepted rather than just displayed. Start with node commands Use a wallet from terminal Open the Rusty Kaspa CLI, read its help output, confirm which network it's pointed at, and hold off on signing until you know where keys are stored. Start with kaspa-cli Practice safely Testnet and TN12 coins carry no value and exist for learning. Break things there first. Start with testnet Build app checks Use wRPC and accepted-transaction replay to prove a txid, payload, or output actually landed, instead of taking an app's word for it. Start with wRPC Use a hosted API A documented API covers address history, acceptance checks, and block ranges for a prototype that has no indexer of its own yet. Start with KDP Mental model Verification ladder 1. Explorer An explorer shows whether a transaction appears accepted. It is one interface's read of the chain, not the chain itself. 2. Second source Check a second explorer, API, wallet, or indexer. Two hosted views that disagree are a signal to slow down, not a coincidence to ignore. 3. Your wallet Network, address, balance, transaction history, fee, and signing intent, read from wallet software you control. 4. Your node Run or query a node to check chain state directly, with no hosted interface in between. Climb the ladder when the situation calls for it. A normal payment doesn't need every rung. Hosted API KDP commands and boundaries The Kaspa Developer Platform is a hosted API for chain data, transaction checks, block queries, and a node RPC proxy. It works for prototypes, dashboards, exchange and wallet integrations, and second-source checks. POST Transaction acceptance Batch-check txids for acceptance, accepting block hash, and confirmation count. curl --request POST \ --url https://api.kas.fyi/v1/transactions/acceptance \ --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \ --header 'x-api-key: <api-key>' \ --data '{"transactionIds":["<txid>"]}' GET DAA-score blocks Read a bounded DAA-score range. KDP caps each request at 100 scores. curl --request GET \ --url https://api.kas.fyi/v1/blocks/daa-score/{daa_score_start}/{daa_score_end} \ --header 'x-api-key: <api-key>' For paginated jobs, advance the range one block at a time and record the last checked score. GET Blue-score blocks Read blocks by blue score when that's the progress marker your app already tracks. curl --request GET \ --url https://api.kas.fyi/v1/blocks/blue-score/{blue_score_start}/{blue_score_end} \ --header 'x-api-key: <api-key>' GET Address history Large address histories need cursor pagination. Cache results and handle rate limits, or the requests pile up fast. curl --request GET \ --url 'https://api.kas.fyi/v1/addresses/<address>/transactions?limit=100' \ --header 'x-api-key: <api-key>' DATA API data rules Amounts arrive as sompi strings. Hashes are 64-character hex. Addresses carry the kaspa: prefix. Timestamps are Unix milliseconds. 1 KAS = 100000000 SOMPI amount: "31112708372" blockTime: 1749531022210 LIMITS Rate limits and keys Send the API key in x-api-key . A 401 means the key is wrong; a 429 means back off. Watch the rate-limit headers and request-unit cost to see it coming first. ratelimit-limit: 500;w=1 ratelimit-remaining: 490 x-request-cost-ru: 10 BOUNDARY Production boundary API keys, rate limits, pricing, and provider uptime are dependencies on someone else's infrastructure. A production app that needs reliability, privacy, or scale should plan its own node, indexer, or a redundant provider path. KDP is a hosted read path, not a source of truth. Protocol status comes from source, releases, KIPs, nodes, and network evidence. Mainnet Run a Rusty Kaspa node Prerequisites: Docker for the container route, or Rust/Cargo for the source route. A node verifies chain state. It does not create or protect wallet keys on its own. Docker route with persistent storage: docker pull kaspanet/rusty-kaspad:latest mkdir -p ~/kaspa-data docker run -d --name kaspa-node --restart unless-stopped \ -v ~/kaspa-data:/app/data \ -p 16110:16110 -p 16111:16111 -p 17110:17110 -p 18110:18110 \ kaspanet/rusty-kaspad:latest Basic container checks: docker ps docker logs --tail=80 kaspa-node Source-build route from the Rusty Kaspa README: git clone https://github.com/kaspanet/rusty-kaspa cd rusty-kaspa cargo run --release --bin kaspad Mainnet node with UTXO indexing: cargo run --release --bin kaspad -- --utxoindex Use --utxoindex when wallet or UTXO queries need indexed UTXO state. A node that hasn't finished syncing will answer confidently and wrongly, so wait for sync before trusting what it says. Wallet and RPC Open the terminal wallet/RPC path From a Rusty Kaspa checkout: cd cli cargo run --release This is the current entry point into the Rusty Kaspa terminal RPC and wallet runtime. Before creating wallets or signing anything: Check network Confirm mainnet or testnet before creating or importing wallet material. Wrong network, wrong keys. Check files Find where wallet files, keys, and local state actually live before you need them in a hurry. Check intent For every transaction, read the address, amount, fee, network, and whether it's a send, sweep, or self-transfer. Test small Send a tiny amount first, then confirm the accepted txid through an independent source before sending more. wRPC Enable a JSON WebSocket RPC endpoint wRPC is optional and off by default in Rusty Kaspa. For JSON wRPC: cargo run --release --bin kaspad -- --utxoindex --rpclisten-json=default This opens a WebSocket that SDKs and scripts can query for node state. Bind it carefully on public machines: a public RPC endpoint is infrastructure, and exposing it doesn't touch key isolation, signing discipline, or verification, which still have to be handled separately. Use wRPC when an app needs to read accepted transactions, inspect payload-capable routes, or compare indexer state against what the node itself observes. Testnet Practice before mainnet Generic Rusty Kaspa testnet route: cargo run --release --bin kaspad -- --testnet Older hard-fork testnet guides used explicit suffixes, for example: kaspad --testnet --netsuffix=10 --utxoindex cargo run --bin kaspad --release -- --testnet --netsuffix=10 --utxoindex For TN12/Toccata work, check the current netsuffix, release, endpoint, and flags against active public docs before running anything. The older TN10 examples are Crescendo-era context, not current instructions. The Rusty Kaspa tn10-toc2 and tn10-toc3 pre-releases, plus the Testnet-10 REST status endpoint, are the current Testnet-10 Toccata activation and hardening evidence. Builder Evidence connects this site to the TN12 proof lab for accepted testnet examples. TN12 practice Use the proof lab for covenant-shaped testnet work TN12 is where covenant, payload, and replay experiments get tested before they touch mainnet behavior. In the TN12 repo, the basic route is: git clone https://github.com/parker2017code/tn12-covenant-vault-demo cd tn12-covenant-vault-demo npm ci npm run check:all npm run check:tn12 npm run playground:wallets Fund only the printed kaspatest: addresses with faucet tKAS, check txids in the TN12 explorer, and replay before trusting what the app reports as state. Anything run with --submit is a real TN12 broadcast, not a dry run. Status: testnet practice. Mainnet wallet, custody, and Toccata activation claims need mainnet evidence, not testnet results. Toccata reminder Command examples need their own receipts Toccata activated at DAA 474,165,565. This page still needs official mainnet docs and working commands verified against them before it presents anything here as live mainnet instructions. Sources Check these before running commands Kaspa Developer Platform docs.kas.fyi Transaction acceptance DAA-score blocks Blue-score blocks Data types Rate limits Hosted API for address history, transaction acceptance, block ranges, and node RPC proxy access. Good for prototypes and second-source checks. Kaspa Build kaspa.org/build Node, SDK, query, explorer, and testnet entry points. Kaspa Docs docs.kaspa.org Integration docs for RPC, payloads, accepted transactions, and node infrastructure. Rusty Kaspa github.com/kaspanet/rusty-kaspa Current node, wallet, CLI, Docker, and wRPC source commands. TN10 Toccata tests tn10-toc3 release tn10-toc2 release Testnet-10 Toccata activation and hardening schedules. Treat them as testnet evidence and check current release notes before running commands. Releases and explorers Rusty Kaspa releases Kaspa explorer Testnet faucet Keep reading Next pages Previous What can you build on Kaspa now? Builder recipes for reading DAG data, watching accepted transactions, tracking UTXOs, generating receipts, verifying a txid, and replaying TN12 evidence. Next Kaspa solo mining guide Connect an ASIC miner to your own node through the Rusty Kaspa Stratum Bridge. pages.title: Kaspa Solo Mining Guide | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: A Kaspa solo mining guide for connecting an ASIC miner to your own node through the Rusty Kaspa Stratum Bridge.
pages.text: Release prep Kaspa solo mining guide An ASIC and a node don't talk to each other directly. Your miner speaks Stratum; your Kaspa node speaks Kaspa RPC. The Rusty Kaspa Stratum Bridge is the translator that sits between them. Status checked June 30, 2026: Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 works as the Toccata upgrade release. The Rusty Kaspa Stratum Bridge is marked beta in the official docs. Toccata activated at DAA 474,165,565, once mainnet crossed the activation score. Start Windows macOS / Linux Miner setup Sources Plain version What you are building Miner The ASIC does the hashing. Its web screen usually asks for a pool URL, username, and password. Bridge The Rusty Kaspa Stratum Bridge accepts the miner connection and talks to a Kaspa node. Node The node hands the bridge block templates and takes back solved blocks. Wallet address The address in the miner username is where a solo block reward lands if the miner finds a block. A miner can submit shares for a long stretch without finding a block. Shares only prove the miner is talking to the bridge. A block reward arrives when the hardware finds a valid block, and solo variance means that can take a while even on working hardware. Quick path The beginner setup One computer runs both the node and bridge. Keep two terminal windows open on that computer, then open the miner's web screen in a browser. Download the Rusty Kaspa zip for the node computer. Extract the zip and open a terminal in that folder. Terminal window A runs kaspad . Leave it open. Terminal window B runs stratum-bridge . Leave it open. The bridge dashboard opens at http://127.0.0.1:3030/ on the node computer. The miner points to the node computer's local IP plus port 5555 . The miner username is the Kaspa receive address plus a worker name. The dashboard should show a worker, shares, and hashrate. Keep the node, bridge, and miner on the same local network for the first setup. Do not expose RPC, dashboard, or Stratum ports to the public internet while learning. What you need Before touching the miner ASIC An IceRiver, Bitmain, Goldshell, or another compatible Kaspa ASIC. The bridge docs also list BzMiner support. Node computer A computer running Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 or newer. Running bridge and node on the same machine avoids a second network hop while learning. Wallet address A Kaspa address for rewards. Copy it carefully. Never paste a private key into miner or bridge settings. Local IP The node computer's address on the home network, such as 192.168.1.10 . Bridge folder The Rusty Kaspa release archive includes the stratum-bridge binary and the sample config path bridge/config.yaml . Patience Shares can show up steadily while block rewards stay rare. That gap is solo mining variance, not a broken setup. Download Which Rusty Kaspa file do I download? Use the official Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 release page and grab the archive matching the computer that will run the node and bridge. Computer Release asset Windows rusty-kaspa-v2.0.1-win64.zip macOS rusty-kaspa-v2.0.1-osx.zip Linux, 64-bit Intel/AMD rusty-kaspa-v2.0.1-linux-amd64.zip Use the release asset for the operating system in play. Skip the GitHub Source code zip and the WASM SDK zip: those build from source or target browser apps, not this setup. Extract Get from zip file to working folder Every command below runs from the extracted Rusty Kaspa folder, not the zip itself. Nothing in the archive runs until it's unpacked. Windows Right-click the downloaded zip, choose Extract All, then open the extracted folder. Expect to see kaspad.exe , stratum-bridge.exe , and a bridge folder. macOS Double-click the zip (Safari may have already unpacked it). Open the extracted folder and look for kaspad , stratum-bridge , and bridge/config.yaml . Linux Use the file manager's Extract option, or run unzip rusty-kaspa-v2.0.1-linux-amd64.zip . Enter the extracted folder before running any commands. "Open a terminal in that folder" means the extracted Rusty Kaspa folder containing the node, bridge, and bridge/config.yaml , not the zip, not its parent directory. Pick your route Which instructions apply to you? Your setup Use this route Node already runs on Windows Use the Windows bridge command in external-node mode, then point the ASIC at the Windows computer's local IP. Node already runs on macOS or Linux Use the macOS / Linux bridge command in external-node mode, then point the ASIC at that computer's local IP. Rusty Kaspa is downloaded but the node hasn't started yet Start kaspad first, wait for sync, then start the bridge. The bridge should start its own node Use in-process mode from the official bridge docs. The beginner route below uses external-node mode, which assumes a node already running. The node runs on another computer Keep the first attempt on one machine if possible. If the node stays remote, edit the bridge config so kaspad_address points to that node's RPC address. Step 1 Open terminal window A and run the node Get into the extracted Rusty Kaspa folder first. On Windows, open the folder in File Explorer, click the address bar, type powershell , and press Enter. On macOS or Linux, open Terminal, type cd , drag the extracted folder into Terminal, and press Enter. Run the node command for the system in use, and leave this window open. The bridge needs the node running continuously to fetch templates and submit blocks. Windows PowerShell Terminal window A .\kaspad.exe --utxoindex --rpclisten=127.0.0.1:16110 macOS / Linux Terminal window A ./kaspad --utxoindex --rpclisten=127.0.0.1:16110 Templates from an unsynced node point at stale chain state, so let sync finish before judging mining results. If a node already runs with custom flags, keep those flags and add the RPC listen setting only if the bridge can't reach the node. The official bridge docs use 127.0.0.1:16110 for the node RPC address. Step 2A Open terminal window B and run the bridge on Windows PowerShell command, dashboard check, port check, and debug logs. Leave the node running in terminal window A. Open a second PowerShell window in the same extracted Rusty Kaspa folder. Run the bridge in external-node mode. Leave this window open too. .\stratum-bridge.exe --config bridge/config.yaml --node-mode external Open the dashboard in a browser on the node computer: http://127.0.0.1:3030/ To check whether the bridge is listening on port 5555 : netstat -ano | findstr :5555 To turn on more detailed bridge logs before starting it: $env:RUST_LOG="info,kaspa_stratum_bridge=debug" "Cannot find bridge/config.yaml" in PowerShell almost always means the wrong folder. A dashboard that won't open means the sample config didn't load or the bridge process stopped: check the last few lines printed in terminal window B. Step 2B Open terminal window B and run the bridge on macOS or Linux Terminal command, dashboard check, port check, and debug logs. Leave the node running in terminal window A. Open a second Terminal window in the same extracted Rusty Kaspa folder. If needed, allow the binary to run. Run the bridge in external-node mode. Leave this window open too. chmod +x ./stratum-bridge ./stratum-bridge --config bridge/config.yaml --node-mode external Open the dashboard in a browser on the node computer: http://127.0.0.1:3030/ To check whether the bridge is listening on port 5555 : lsof -i :5555 To turn on more detailed bridge logs for one run: RUST_LOG="info,kaspa_stratum_bridge=debug" ./stratum-bridge --config bridge/config.yaml --node-mode external "Cannot find bridge/config.yaml" in Terminal almost always means the wrong folder. On macOS, Gatekeeper may ask for approval before it runs a downloaded binary. Only approve binaries pulled from the official Rusty Kaspa release page. Other route If the bridge should start its own node In-process mode from the official bridge docs. In-process mode, also documented by the bridge, starts kaspad inside the same process as the bridge rather than as a separate program. Windows PowerShell Bridge plus in-process node .\stratum-bridge.exe --config bridge/config.yaml --node-mode inprocess -- --utxoindex --rpclisten=127.0.0.1:16110 macOS / Linux Bridge plus in-process node ./stratum-bridge --config bridge/config.yaml --node-mode inprocess -- --utxoindex --rpclisten=127.0.0.1:16110 The -- separator is not optional. Bridge flags go before it, node flags after. Step 3 Find the node computer's local IP address The miner needs the local network address of the computer running the bridge, usually something like 192.168.x.x or 10.0.x.x . Windows PowerShell or Command Prompt ipconfig Look for the active Wi-Fi or Ethernet adapter and copy the IPv4 Address. macOS Wi-Fi ipconfig getifaddr en0 If Ethernet is active, System Settings can be easier: Network, then your active connection, then Details. Linux Terminal hostname -I Use the address on the same network as your miner. Step 4 Point the ASIC at the bridge Open the miner's web screen. If the miner's IP address isn't known, check the router's connected-device list or the manufacturer's setup tool. Type the miner IP into a browser, sign in, and find the mining or pool configuration page. Use the bridge computer's local IP address and one of the Stratum ports from the sample config, starting with port 5555 . Miner field Put this in Example Pool URL <node-computer-ip>:5555 192.168.1.10:5555 Username / worker kaspa:YOUR_WALLET_ADDRESS.WORKERNAME kaspa:kaspa:qq...abcd.ks0 Password Use the miner UI default if it requires a value. x is common in miner UIs, but the Rusty Kaspa bridge docs define only pool URL and username. A Kaspa address already starts with kaspa: , so the username field ends up looking like kaspa:kaspa:... . That duplication matches the official bridge format; it's not a typo. Some miner screens expect a URL prefix instead. The official bridge docs give the pool URL as <your_pc_IPv4>:<stratum_port> ; if a miner rejects that format, check its manual for the exact Stratum URL syntax it wants. Miner brands What changes by miner or software type? IceRiver, Bitmain, BzMiner, Goldshell, and field-name differences. The bridge detects several miner and mining-software types automatically and adjusts protocol handling per type. The setup screen itself still belongs to the miner manufacturer, so field labels vary. IceRiver Listed in the bridge docs; these miners require extranonce plus a single hex string job format. Bitmain Bitmain and GodMiner are listed; these miners use no extranonce, with array plus timestamp job format. BzMiner Listed in the bridge docs; requires extranonce plus a single hex string job format. Goldshell Listed in the bridge docs; requires extranonce plus a single hex string job format. Whatever the brand, the fields that matter stay the same: pool URL, username or wallet field, and a password only if the miner UI demands one. Ports Pick the first port Start with 5555, then use lower difficulty ports only for troubleshooting. The sample config exposes several Stratum ports, each tuned to a different worker difficulty. Start with 5555 . Drop to a lower-difficulty port only when troubleshooting a connection or matching a weaker worker per the bridge docs. Port Sample config purpose 5559 Very low-difficulty workers. 5560 Low-difficulty workers. 5561 Medium-difficulty workers. 5555 Higher-difficulty workers. Start here for a normal ASIC setup. 5556 , 5557 , 5558 Higher difficulty ports. Step 5 Check that it is working Bridge window, dashboard, miner screen, and node checks. Bridge window Should keep running and show miner connection or job activity. Dashboard Open http://127.0.0.1:3030/ and look for active workers, shares, hashrate, and recent activity. Miner screen Should show an active pool, accepted shares, and hashrate. Node Should stay synced and keep receiving network updates. Accepted shares confirm the setup is wired correctly. They are not the reward event: a found block is. A correctly configured rig can run for a long stretch with steady shares and zero blocks; that is solo variance, not a fault. Toccata Toccata mining checks Version, activation record, post-Toccata template fields, and testnet checks. Post-activation block templates can carry new transaction fields. The official node guide warns pools and custom mining stacks to preserve those fields all the way from block template to solved block submission, or risk submitting an invalid block. Upgrade Use Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 or newer for the node and bridge path. Activation record Mainnet activation crossed DAA score 474,165,565 . Check Toccata status for post-activation checks. Template fields Custom mining software must preserve post-Toccata fields: transaction version, storage mass, compute budget, and covenant outputs. Test first Run it on Testnet-10 where possible before trusting a mainnet mining path built after the activation score. Fixes If it does not connect Pool dead, empty dashboard, bridge-node RPC, firewall, rewards, and activation-day checks. Symptom Check Miner says pool dead Use the node computer's local IP address, not 127.0.0.1 . That address points the miner back at itself. Dashboard is empty Check the bridge is still running, the miner is on the same network, and the pool URL uses a port from the sample config. Bridge cannot reach node Confirm the node is running with RPC at 127.0.0.1:16110 , or update the bridge config to the node's actual RPC address. Firewall blocks connection Allow the Stratum port on the node computer for the local network. No rewards Check shares first. Rewards need a solved block, and solo variance can leave a working rig without one for a long time. Toccata activation day Recheck versions and logs. Past the activation score, a block that strips new fields is invalid. Safer setup What to avoid Network exposure, wallet safety, shares versus blocks, and Toccata compatibility. Network exposure Keep node RPC, the bridge dashboard, and Stratum ports on the local network while learning. Exposing them publicly invites avoidable trouble. Wallet safety Use a public Kaspa receive address for the miner username. Never paste a seed phrase or private key into miner, bridge, or dashboard settings. Shares versus blocks Accepted shares only confirm the miner is talking to the bridge. They say nothing about a payout timeline. Solo rewards need a found block. Toccata compatibility After Toccata activation, run current node, bridge, pool, and custom mining software. Older software can drop new block-template fields and submit invalid blocks. pages.text: Builder evidence How to prove a Kaspa builder claim A builder claim is not a product. It becomes credible only when a reviewer can see the status label, the source, the artifact, the user-visible result, and the blocker list: all five, not a selection. Use this for demo proof. Use Claims Checker for protocol status. Use Reality Check for app or product pitches before they become public claims. Proof ladder Claim Write the exact sentence a reader would believe or repeat to someone else, not a paraphrase of it. Status lane Live, testnet-only, targeted, roadmap, research, wrong, or unsupported: pick the one that's true today. Source Point to the strongest available source for that lane, not the most convenient one. Artifact Name the txid, branch, release, KIP, demo, indexer result, or command output: something checkable. User-visible result State what a wallet user, builder, miner, or operator can actually observe right now. Remaining blocker List what still stands between this and a broader public claim. Evidence lanes Kaspa claims split into mainnet features, near-term upgrades, and early design work , and each lane demands a different proof level. Live: code merged, activated on mainnet, available to builders now Targeted: scheduled for near-term release or being implemented Roadmap: architecture approved or research-backed; scheduling still missing Research: in exploration, no timeline or approval yet Builder tooling, open code, and mainnet activation are three different states. Merged code proves the code exists. It doesn't prove mainnet activation. Advanced state-transition proof note State-transition proof models follow one pattern: selected-parent root plus current root plus leaf write witnesses. That keeps validation local to the single transition. Clients never have to maintain the whole incremental SMT. pages.title: What Crypto Is Actually Good For | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: A tempered guide to where crypto is useful, where it is weak, and where shared records without one operator fit.
pages.text: Crypto reality check What crypto is good for Crypto earns its cost when strangers need one shared record of who owns what, and no single company, bank, platform, or government is trusted to run it. Crypto is useful when strangers need one shared record of ownership and rules, and no single party should control it. Summary: use crypto when a shared record without an operator is worth what it costs. Skip it when a normal database, a trusted operator, or a court already does the job better. The primitive A blockchain is a costly shared ledger NIST's definition is the plain one: a tamper-evident, tamper-resistant digital ledger, implemented in a distributed way, usually without a central repository or authority. Bitcoin, stablecoins, NFTs, tokenized securities, DeFi, DAOs, and smart contracts are all just applications built on that one narrow idea. The question worth asking is not "can this use a blockchain." It's whether strangers need to coordinate around ownership, transfer, and rules without a company, bank, broker, or state as the final word. Yes, and crypto is doing real work. No, and it's usually a slower, more expensive database wearing a costume. Where crypto fits Where crypto is actually strong Bearer digital assets Whoever holds the private key controls the asset, the same way whoever holds a banknote controls it. Holding BTC or KAS directly means an exchange freeze can't touch it: self-custody, not a feature request. Cross-border stablecoin settlement Stablecoins are imperfect dollar instruments, and still one of crypto's clearest product-market fits. A freelancer gets paid from abroad in minutes when the local banking rail would take days or simply not clear. Tokenized collateral and funds Tokenized Treasuries, money-market funds, and institutional collateral get programmable ownership and round-the-clock settlement. The legal wrapper still controls what the asset actually is in court: the token is a record of it, not the asset. On-chain markets Decentralized exchanges and lending protocols work best when the assets, settlement, collateral, and execution already live on-chain: swapping one on-chain asset for another without routing through a broker. Programmable escrow Smart contracts hold up when the condition is objective and checkable on-chain: both parties signed, a vesting date arrived, collateral crossed a threshold, asset and payment settled atomically. Digital provenance NFTs earn their keep as records of provenance, access, membership, ticketing, or portable digital objects. Copyright, legal ownership, and cultural value still need support from outside the chain. Open-network incentives Tokens coordinate validators, storage providers, liquidity providers, developers, and compute markets when no single company should be the one employing all of them. Credible neutrality A public protocol lets independent teams build wallets, clients, markets, analytics, and apps without asking a platform owner for permission or trusting one database operator's uptime. Bad fit Where crypto is usually weak Normal domestic payments Cards, instant payments, Pix, UPI, SEPA, Zelle, and Apple Pay beat crypto on UX, refunds, fraud handling, identity checks, and customer support: the things a domestic payment actually needs. Universal databases Most companies need a normal database. If one entity already controls the users, data, permissions, and rules, a blockchain just adds cost and complexity to a problem that was already solved. Replacing courts Code enforces simple rules well. It cannot handle fraud, coercion, mistaken transfers, bankruptcy, inheritance, divorce claims, property disputes, identity theft, or contract ambiguity: the cases courts exist for. Private records Public ledgers are pseudonymous by default, not private. Link one address to a person or company and the entire transaction graph becomes visible. Supply-chain truth machines A blockchain preserves whatever gets entered. If someone lies about where the tuna came from, the chain preserves the lie perfectly. It never inspected the tuna. Unsecured consumer credit Normal lending runs on identity, income, credit history, collections, bankruptcy law, and courts. Overcollateralized on-chain lending is a different product wearing the same name. Tokenizing everything A token doesn't solve legal ownership, custody, inspection, liens, taxes, fraud, transfer restrictions, or jurisdiction-specific enforcement on its own. Weak products with tokens A token is not a business model. Plenty of projects use one to subsidize fake demand, paper over weak economics, or move the risk onto retail buyers. Tradeoffs What you get and what it costs Property Benefit Cost Self-custody You control assets directly Lose keys, lose funds Irreversibility Final settlement No easy fraud recovery Public ledger Transparency and auditability Privacy leakage Permissionless access Anyone can participate Scams and low-quality projects flourish Programmability Automated financial logic Smart-contract and oracle risk Decentralization No single operator Slower governance and worse UX Token incentives Bootstraps open networks Speculation and misaligned incentives Global settlement Cross-border access Regulatory and compliance complexity Crypto gets called "trustless." It isn't. It's trust-minimized in specific, narrow dimensions, while the trust it removes from a bank teller gets relocated into code, wallets, bridges, oracles, governance votes, stablecoin issuers, custodians, frontends, and law. Decision rule Crypto makes sense when at least three are true Run any crypto project through this list. Fewer than three honest checks, and the project is probably bolting crypto onto a problem that never needed it. Shared ledger across parties that do not fully trust each other Users need to verify the rules themselves Assets must move globally, 24/7 Users need self-custody Users need censorship resistance The asset is digital or legally represented digitally Settlement speed is worth limited reversibility The product needs composability with on-chain systems A token is necessary to coordinate incentives Crypto probably doesn't make sense when one company already controls the whole system, users mainly want refunds and customer support, the data is private or legally sensitive, the hard part is verifying a real-world fact rather than a digital one, courts have to enforce ownership anyway, a normal database would work, or the token exists mainly to raise money. Bridge to Kaspa Judge Kaspa where shared records need neutrality Kaspa's lane is narrow: Proof of Work, self-custody, global settlement, censorship resistance, fast confirmation feel, and later, apps that prove their own rules. That's the set of problems where crypto's cost is worth paying. A credible shared ledger still has to solve ordering, double-spend resistance, resource pricing, validation, storage growth, pruning, timing, and finality. Kaspa's blockDAG, UTXO model, mass rules, pruning commitments, and covenant roadmap are all direct answers to those problems, not marketing around them. Live features, near-term implementation, roadmap architecture, and research get kept apart deliberately. The facts on the ground are already enough to evaluate Kaspa; padding the page with every possible future claim would only make it harder to check. Continue to the Kaspa design case Source notes Sources for the reality check NIST IR 8202 for the blockchain-as-distributed-ledger definition. World Bank Remittance Prices Worldwide for remittance-cost context. Chainalysis 2024 Latin America report for stablecoin usage in Argentina and Brazil. IMF Understanding Stablecoins for stablecoin policy risks. BIS Annual Economic Report 2025, Chapter III for tokenized monetary and financial infrastructure. Securitize / PR Newswire on BUIDL surpassing $1B AUM as a dated institutional-tokenization milestone. BIS Annual Economic Report 2022, Chapter III for the critique of crypto as the basis for a monetary system. Next step Pick your missing layer Records, keys, blocks, consensus, tokens, or market cap still fuzzy? Start from zero. Already solid on the lane crypto belongs in? Go straight to Kaspa.
