pages.title: Kaspa Status | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: What is live, targeted, roadmap, and research on Kaspa right now, checked against mainnet, releases, and KIPs.
pages.text: Current status Kaspa current status Kaspa lets blocks mined at the same time survive instead of orphaning one of them. Its blockDAG keeps every honest block that miners produce; GHOSTDAG then orders them into one UTXO history. What runs on mainnet today and what is still roadmap architecture get different labels below. Legend Live Targeted Roadmap Research Not live Checked: June 30, 2026 at 16:19 UTC. Public mainnet REST checks reported kaspa-mainnet , virtual DAA above the activation score, matching block and header counts, about 27.545 billion KAS from the supply endpoint, and a 2.59565436 KAS block reward. Toccata: Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 is the current Toccata release; v2.0.0 set activation at DAA score 474,165,565. Use Toccata status for post-activation checks. Freshness triggers What would change this page Toccata activation Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 is the current Toccata release. v2.0.0 set activation at DAA 474,165,565. What comes next: upgraded-node behavior, accepted v1 transactions, wallet support, explorer support, SDK support, app receipts, and user activity. Mainnet behavior An accepted mainnet transaction running the new rules beats any number of testnet examples or roadmap posts. L1 source drift Mainnet API readings, Rusty Kaspa releases, KIP states, and emission-schedule checkpoints move fast enough that exact values need a fresh check before quoting. Use Status Updates for dated snapshots. This page holds the current wording. Usable today What users can do now Hold and transfer Send, receive, and self-custody KAS on the live Proof-of-Work UTXO blockDAG. Verify and observe Run or study nodes, explorers, visualizers, pruning behavior, and GHOSTDAG ordering. Mine or study mining Kaspa is ASIC-mined today. The solo mining guide covers miner-to-node setup; current dashboards cover mining economics and distribution. Build around the live lane Wallet UX, payment flows, analytics, education, and infrastructure can build on today's 10 BPS foundation. Check the L1 state A public REST reading is a snapshot, not a claim. Cross it against a node, release notes, KIP status, and accepted mainnet behavior first. Snapshot Status in one table Live mainnet behavior, testnet evidence, targeted upgrade work, roadmap architecture, and research are five different claims. Collapsing them into one is where most Kaspa misinformation starts. Live network PoW, UTXO, GHOSTDAG, Crescendo 10 BPS, and base real-time PoW framing. June 29 L1 check Mainnet API read virtual DAA score 473,005,279, 1,102,009 blocks, about 27.542 billion KAS, and 2.59565436 KAS per block. Emission path Emission steps down monthly, not off a cliff. May 2026 sits at 27.5 KAS/sec; June 7 drops to 25.9565436 KAS/sec. Feature / idea Status Plain meaning Anchor source Proof of Work Live Kaspa is mined, not staked. Work and issuance never depend on a validator identity set. rusty-kaspa UTXO model Live Kaspa tracks spendable outputs, not account balances. That's the same model Bitcoin uses; Ethereum tracks balances instead. rusty-kaspa GHOSTDAG Live GHOSTDAG keeps blocks that lose the race to be first instead of discarding them, then orders every kept block into one history. Kaspa Research Crescendo 10 BPS Live 10 blocks per second is live. Michael Sutton put the throughput gain at roughly 8-9x and the confirmation-time improvement around 30%. Neither figure is instant finality, and a flat "10x faster confirmations" claim overstates his own numbers. rusty-kaspa releases ; Crescendo roadmap note ; Kaspa.org lore June 29 L1 snapshot Live snapshot Mainnet REST readout at 16:19 UTC: virtual DAA above 474,165,565, matching block and header counts, about 27.545 billion KAS from the supply endpoint, 2.59565436 KAS per block. These numbers move by the hour; recheck before quoting them. mainnet blockDAG API ; supply API ; block reward API Emission schedule Live design The schedule steps down monthly: 27.5 KAS/sec from May 8, 2026, 25.9565436 KAS/sec from June 7, 24.49971475 KAS/sec from July 7. There is no single-day July cliff. Kaspa Wiki tokenomics ; block reward API Base RTD framing Live Real-time decentralization is Hashdag's name for Kaspa's core trade: Bitcoin-style PoW security and censorship resistance, with confirmations that feel seconds-scale under normal network conditions. Kaspa.org lore ; hashd.ag/raw Toccata Live protocol Hard fork for L1 spend rules, asset rules, Silverscript, ZK proof checks, sequencing commitments, standalone based-zk applications, and vProgs groundwork. Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 is the current Toccata release; v2.0.0 set mainnet activation at DAA 474,165,565. v2.0.1 release ; v2.0.0 activation release ; Toccata guide ; tn10-toc3 release ; Kaspa KIPs vProgs Roadmap Apps that prove richer logic while sharing Kaspa ordering, without turning L1 into a single global execution VM. vProgs repo ; programmability docs Native DeFi Roadmap A design target that follows Toccata-era L1 foundations. A live Kaspa-native app layer needs shipped apps and usage evidence, not just the architecture for it. Design case DAGKnight Research A parameterless, adaptive consensus direction. It does not run mainnet today; GHOSTDAG does. Kaspa.org lore ; hashd.ag 100 BPS / partition-resilient payments Research Kaspa.org places 10-millisecond blocks, 100 BPS, and partition-resilient local payments in a proposed 2027 hard-fork bucket. No specification, code, release, or activation evidence exists yet. Kaspa.org lore RTD-derived oracle / TangVM flows Research Apps can build oracle, TangVM, attestation, and coordination-market systems over Kaspa primitives. The protocol does not ship any of them as products. hashd.ag/raw Common misconceptions Statements that need context or measurement Most Kaspa confusion comes from one move: blending a live protocol fact, a test result, a public target, and a project headline into a single sentence. Pull them apart before repeating a claim. Claim people repeat Measured version Consequence Mainnet speed means a fixed huge TPS number. 10 BPS is live. Simple-payment capacity runs roughly 2.5k to 3.4k TPS depending on transaction shape; covenant apps, ZK proofs, tokens, and vProg-style systems each need their own workload number. See Kaspa TPS Explained . One number turns a real technical edge into a brittle marketing claim. Block rate alone gives an exact finality multiplier. Faster blocks improve inclusion and capacity. Confirmation confidence is a separate, probabilistic question. Users care about both: when a payment shows up, and how sure they should be it stays. Testnet or lab numbers are mainnet guarantees. Testnets and experiments are signals, not commitments. They need a current source check before they become a live public claim. Future capability, engineering tests, and shipped network behavior are three different things. Real-time means instant finality. Real-time describes the fast-PoW user feel and the decentralization goal. It does not claim every transaction is instantly irreversible. The pitch stays strong without overselling settlement certainty. DAGKnight, Toccata, vProgs, or native DeFi are live because code or talks exist. Code, talks, branches, and demos prove work happened. Activation or production status needs stronger evidence than that. Development evidence sits below release or activation evidence, not on top of it. Toccata means one atomic action can already span several independent apps. Toccata is the foundation for covenant rules, ZK proof checks, sequencing commitments, and based-zk applications. Full cross-app atomic composition is later vProgs work. Fast L1 coordination and same-operation app composability are different claims. July 2026 is a sudden emission cliff. Kaspa emission steps down monthly: 27.5 KAS/sec from May 8, 25.9565436 from June 7, 24.49971475 from July 7. The scarcity story is the schedule, not a one-day cliff. Open KIPs or branches prove an upgrade is activated. Open KIPs, branches, and pre-releases are development evidence. Activation needs release artifacts, activation parameters, upgraded node behavior, and observable mainnet behavior. The upgrade story stays tied to primary L1 evidence instead of roadmap momentum. Implementation evidence Code evidence Code and pull requests show work in progress. A mainnet label needs more: a release, an activation record, upgraded-node behavior, or observable network behavior. Open code and implementation evidence Track Recent public evidence How to read it Toccata / Silverscript TN12 dependency sync , KCC20 bootstrap fixes , and book/build fixes landed May 4-5, 2026. TN12 field testing surfaced developer-ergonomics issues around covenant and ZK opcode use. The v1.3.0-toc.5 pre-release sanity-tested mainnet pre-activation compatibility. The v2.0.0 release sets mainnet activation at DAA score 474,165,565; v2.0.1 is the current Toccata release. The Toccata node setup guide adds operator guidance for upgrades, fee policy, API field changes, and Testnet-10 checks. The merged Rusty Kaspa ZK SDK PR adds an R0ScriptBuilder wrapper for turning RISC Zero receipts into Kaspa scripts. The tn10-toc3 pre-release scheduled final TN10 hardening; a June 29 check of Testnet-10 REST status showed virtual DAA 503,616,667. Activated mainnet release evidence: release notes, activation parameters, the operator guide, TN10/TN12 testing, SDK and tooling prep. After activation, the next checks are wallets, explorers, examples, and accepted mainnet transactions. Toccata KIPs Kaspa.org Build lists sequencing commitments in the Toccata bundle and labels it live on TN12 ahead of mainnet activation. Raw KIP checks on June 29 showed KIP-16 and KIP-20 as proposed plus implemented and activated in TN10, and KIP-17 and KIP-21 as implemented and activated in TN10. Open KIP PRs add important future context: KIP-24 specifies transaction version 1 fields and hashing for compute budgets, covenant bindings, user lanes, and ZK-friendly payload/rest txids; KIP-22 proposes P2MR ScriptPublicKey work for quantum-resistance and MAST-style scripts. Design and testnet implementation evidence. TN10 KIP status alone doesn't set the mainnet label; that comes from the activation record and observable network behavior. Open KIP PRs KIP-24 is open for transaction version 1 fields and hashing; its draft text says v1 transactions add per-input compute budgets, optional output covenant bindings, user-lane subnetworks, and a BLAKE3 payload/rest txid split for ZK and based-executor workflows. KIP-22 is open for P2MR ScriptPublicKey, described as a Merkle-root pay-to-script form meant to hide public keys until spend time and support quantum-resistance and MAST-style conditional scripts. Design and implementation evidence, not merged-KIP or mainnet activation evidence. KIP-24 sits closer to Toccata transaction plumbing; KIP-22 is future cryptography and script-design work. Argent michaelsutton/argent is a June 2026 experimental actor-style frontend for Silverscript covenant contracts. Its README describes actors, state, transitions, named emits, terminal become dispatch, and generated Silverscript for examples such as Stones and Tickets. Fresh research and tooling evidence, explicitly a prototype. No audit, no production readiness, no stable ABI, no generated transaction builder, no mainnet activation evidence. vProgs The kaspanet/vprogs README describes an early-development Rust framework for based computation on Kaspa, with core, storage, state, scheduling, transaction-runtime, and node layers. A June 18 merge, Feat: Settlement into Covenants , gathered settlement-covenant work, transaction/batch/aggregation provers, SMT support, L1 bridge plumbing, and RISC Zero backend work into master. Roadmap implementation progress. Builders can study and experiment with the framework now. Production Kaspa app paths and native DeFi still need their own shipped evidence. See vProgs Explained . DAGKnight The public rusty-kaspa dagknight branch shows March 22, 2026 commits for free-search support, ranking/search refinements, conflict-zone work, tie-breaking placeholder, and UMC majority-coverage movement. Research and prototype evidence. Mainnet still runs GHOSTDAG; live finality and higher-BPS claims need their own activation evidence. Builder tooling kaspanet/kaspa-python-sdk is now a standalone public SDK repo. The v2.0.0 release added Toccata-aligned support and the full Rusty Kaspa managed-wallet API for Python. The v2.0.1 release adds get_seq_commit_lane_proof , SMT sync progress events, covenant-binding fixes, and a Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 dependency bump. Developer-tooling progress that helps Python builders and integrators prepare for Toccata-era wallet, UTXO, lane-proof, and covenant workflows. Protocol-upgrade status still comes from node, KIP, and activation evidence, not the SDK. Infrastructure indexes rusty-kaspa PR #860 is open for review. It proposes an optional --txindex , a GetTransaction RPC path, inclusion and acceptance metadata, live updates from consensus notifications, resync from scratch, and pruning tied to retention-root changes. pages.text: Claims reference Claims need a status label An unlabeled claim spreads confusion by default. Put it in one lane first: live mainnet, testnet evidence, targeted upgrade, roadmap, research, unsupported, or out of scope. Last checked: June 30, 2026. Use claims checker Open current status Open sources How to use it Start with the claim, then ask what evidence it has Live Behavior available on Kaspa mainnet now: Proof of Work, UTXO ownership, GHOSTDAG ordering, Crescendo-era 10 BPS, Toccata's activated covenant layer, wallets, nodes, and explorers. Out of L1 scope App and project catalog context stays outside this site's status labels unless the claim is specifically about L1 transaction data, accepted transactions, or miner fees. Testnet-only TN10/TN12 activation or covenant proof work, accepted testnet transactions, rejected mutation cases, developer-flow evidence. None of it proves mainnet activation on its own. Targeted Near-term work where release artifacts, activation parameters, or implementation evidence exist, but mainnet behavior still needs a current check. Roadmap vProgs , full cross-app composition, and richer app architecture that still need shipped software and users. Research DAGKnight, 100 BPS research, partition-resilient payments, RTD-derived oracle/attestation flows, TangVM, and coordination-market systems. Copy rules Status comes first Topic Safe wording Avoid Finality Fast mined inclusion and probabilistic confirmation confidence. Instant finality or immediate irreversibility. Polychain Polychain belongs in the VC-funded DAGLabs prehistory. Premine and pre-sale allocation claims need their own token-allocation evidence. Ignoring Polychain context, or treating it as proof of a premine. Fair launch No premine, insider allocation, or pre-sales: every coin came from mining, including the post-launch DAGLabs/Polychain-related early mining estimate. DAGLabs/Polychain premine language, flawless distribution, or no early contributor mining. Original codebase Original Kaspad was Golang, source-backed as an adaptation of btcd . A specific Bitcoin Core version without a durable source. App and project tooling Out of scope unless the claim is specifically about L1 transaction data, accepted transactions, or miner fees. App activity proves mainnet activation or native smart contracts. TN10 Testnet-10 Toccata activation and hardening evidence, including tn10-toc2 and tn10-toc3. TN10 test activation is mainnet activation. TN12 Testnet evidence for covenant developer flows and opcode testing. TN12 txids or rejections prove mainnet covenant enforcement. Toccata Live. Activated at DAA score 474,165,565; v2.0.1 is the current release. Wallet, explorer, SDK, and app adoption are separate checks, still open. Treating activation as pending, or treating downstream adoption as automatic. Emission Steps down monthly: 27.5 KAS/sec from May 2026, 25.9565436 from June 7, 24.49971475 from July 7. July 2026 is a one-day emission cliff. vProgs Later app architecture for apps that prove richer logic while sharing Kaspa ordering. Not on testnet yet. Mainnet app infrastructure has already shipped. Argent Experimental actor-style frontend for Silverscript covenant contracts. Argent proves production smart contracts, audits, a stable ABI, or mainnet activation. DAGKnight Research-stage, early prototype. Not testnet-ready. DAGKnight is current mainnet behavior, or close to shipping. ZK hooks A proof verifies computation over chosen inputs. External facts still need their own anchor. A proof alone proves prices, other chains, reserves, or real-world events. Editor rule One sentence test catches most mistakes If a sentence adds no actor, action, evidence, status label, constraint, consequence, distinction, or reader judgment, delete it. Tie public wording back to Status, Claims, and Sources. One status label, stated once, then the point directly. pages.text: Toccata status Kaspa Toccata status Toccata is live on Kaspa mainnet. It activated at DAA score 474,165,565 on June 30, 2026, adding covenant-style programmability to Kaspa's L1. Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 is the current upgrade release; v2.0.0 set the activation parameters. Summary: Toccata adds Kaspa L1 covenants, covenant IDs, ZK proof hooks, sequencing commitments, and based-app foundations. Next to check: upgraded-node behavior, wallets, explorers, SDKs, examples, real app use. Read the limits too: Risks and Open Questions covers adoption and roadmap execution; Smart-Contract Status separates Toccata from mature live app infrastructure. Current state Status by area Upgrade release Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 is the current Toccata upgrade release; v2.0.0 remains the activation-parameter release. Activation Toccata activated on mainnet at DAA score 474,165,565, June 30, 2026, roughly 16:15 UTC. Downstream layers Separate from activation itself: upgraded-node behavior, transaction fields, covenant data, ZK proof paths, wallet support, explorer support, builder examples. Confirmed: public API checks read kaspa-mainnet above DAA 474,165,565, with block and header counts still climbing past the score. Area Status What it means Mainnet release Released Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 published June 15, 2026 as a Toccata maintenance release. v2.0.0 published June 5, 2026 as the Mainnet Toccata Release, setting activation at DAA score 474,165,565, roughly June 30, 2026 at 16:15 UTC. Mainnet activation Activated Toccata is live: mainnet REST checks read virtual DAA above 474,165,565, with block and header counts climbing past the score. Node upgrades and accepted mainnet transactions using the new fields are the next layer to verify. TN10 activation tests Testnet The tn10-toc2 pre-release put Testnet-10 activation at DAA score 467,579,632. tn10-toc3 scheduled final Toccata ZK hardening at DAA score 476,232,000. A June 29 check of the Testnet-10 REST API read virtual DAA 503,616,667, past both scores. TN12 covenant testing Testnet Developer-flow and opcode testing evidence. It does not change mainnet status. Silverscript Targeted A high-level scripting language and examples for native Kaspa Script work. Toccata KIPs Activation bundle KIP-16, KIP-17, KIP-20, and KIP-21 are the activated bundle. A June 29 raw KIP check found KIP-16 and KIP-20 proposed, implemented, and activated in TN10; KIP-17 and KIP-21 implemented and activated in TN10. Argent Research Michael Sutton's Argent repo is an experimental actor-style frontend for Silverscript covenant contracts, early research and tooling work. Production readiness and activation are separate evidence bars, both still unmet. ZK SDK Tooling The merged Rusty Kaspa ZK SDK PR adds an R0ScriptBuilder wrapper for RISC Zero proof scripts. It improves builder ergonomics; production ZK apps still need their own receipts and user flows. zk verification hooks Protocol surface A script can verify a proof. It still can't anchor external facts on its own. Transaction v1 / KIP-24 Open PR KIP-24 is open for transaction version 1 fields and hashing: compute budgets, covenant bindings, user lanes, and a BLAKE3 payload/rest txid split for ZK and based-executor workflows. Full vProgs composition Roadmap Later architecture for richer app-to-app behavior . Toccata's activated surface is narrower than that. What changes Toccata adds expressiveness Toccata adds L1 rule surfaces: covenant scripting, covenant IDs, ZK proof verification, sequencing commitments, foundations for based apps. It does not turn Kaspa into an EVM, and full vProgs still need their own roadmap and activation evidence. Covenants Constrained UTXO spends for vaults, escrow paths, asset rules, and other bounded money rules. Covenant IDs Consensus-tracked covenant lineage gives state membership a protocol-level reference. ZK proof checks A script can verify selected proof systems. App truth still rests on the statement and inputs being proved, not the proof mechanism alone. KIP-21 lanes App-local activity commitments let a prover follow its own lane instead of the whole DAG. Based apps Standalone apps can anchor state to Kaspa ordering, proofs, settlement, or exits. vProgs later Full app-to-app composition stays future architecture. Toccata's mainnet activation covers a narrower slice. Explainer: Toccata Explained . Wording Claim wording Toccata is live. It activated at DAA score 474,165,565. Wallets, explorers, SDKs, examples, and app use are separate, still-developing claims. What it can enable Vault rules, asset rules, escrow paths, assurance contracts, proof checks, sequencing commitments, standalone based-app foundations. Separate evidence needed Mature native DeFi, full vProgs , full app-to-app atomic composition, and mainnet production readiness don't follow automatically from activation. What to verify next Node behavior, transaction submission, wallet support, explorer support, SDK support, mainnet transactions using the new rules. Operator checklist Who needs to check their path The Toccata guide reads as an operator and integrator checklist. After activation, the work shifts from upgrade readiness to field checks: node behavior, transaction submission, wallet support, explorer support, app receipts. Ordinary users No node action needed unless they run infrastructure. Holding or sending KAS through a normal wallet is a different job than maintaining consensus or service infrastructure. Node operators Run Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 or newer. The node database upgrade only goes one way: the only path back is a resync. Wallets and submitters Use fee estimation, or update fixed-fee code to 100 sompi * max(compute grams, 2 * transaction bytes) . Upgraded nodes apply the higher standard-fee policy to direct RPC submissions. Exchanges and indexers Update SDKs or regenerate bindings, then handle transaction version 1 , storageMass / storage_mass , computeBudget , output covenants, and UTXO covenant_id . Miners and pools Test block templates, job distribution, solved block reconstruction, and SubmitBlock against Testnet-10. A block that strips post-Toccata fields can turn invalid after the activation score. Pool accounting Check GetBlockRewardInfo , and GetSeqCommitLaneProof where lane-proof data matters. Infrastructure detail, but the kind that breaks payouts if skipped. Primary references: Toccata node setup guide , Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 , and Go Kaspad v0.12.23 . pages.title: Kaspa Finality: Fast Inclusion vs Confirmation Confidence | Kaspa Explained
pages.h1: A transaction can land in a block before you finish reading this sentence. That is not the same as final.
pages.description: A transaction can land in a block in under a second on Kaspa. It still isn't final the moment it lands. How GHOSTDAG ordering, 10 BPS, and accumulated work turn inclusion into confidence.
pages.text: Claim correction A transaction can land in a block before you finish reading this sentence. That is not the same as final. Kaspa mines blocks fast enough that inclusion feels instant, and GHOSTDAG keeps ordering parallel blocks as they arrive instead of forcing miners to wait their turn. What it doesn't do is make a transaction irreversible the moment it's included. Reversal risk drops as more proof-of-work piles on top of it. Summary: Kaspa has fast mined inclusion and confirmation confidence that rises with accumulated work. "Real-time" describes inclusion speed, not finality. Payment path Five steps from broadcast to trustworthy 1 Seen A wallet or node picks up the broadcast transaction. 2 Included A miner mines it into a proof-of-work block. 3 Ordered The block joins the DAG alongside blocks mined in parallel, and GHOSTDAG orders the history. 4 Accepted Nodes accept the ordered transaction under Kaspa's consensus rules. 5 Confidence Reversal risk keeps falling as more blocks stack proof-of-work on top of it. Copy block How to state the claim Kaspa's 10 BPS blockDAG and GHOSTDAG ordering cut payment latency: a transaction can be mined into a block in a fraction of a second. Confirmation confidence still rises probabilistically as more work accumulates on top of it. Shortcut Safer version Kaspa payments are irreversible immediately. Inclusion is fast; reversal risk drops as confirmation confidence rises. 10 BPS means 10x finality. 10 BPS is live and speeds up inclusion. Finality confidence still depends on accumulated proof-of-work and network conditions. Real-time means irreversible now. Real-time describes how fast a block gets mined, not how final the transaction inside it is. pages.title: GHOSTDAG Explained | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: How GHOSTDAG orders parallel proof-of-work blocks in Kaspa's blockDAG, why losing blocks still count toward security, and what it doesn't buy you: instant finality.
pages.text: Protocol explainer GHOSTDAG explained Kaspa's losing blocks still count toward security. GHOSTDAG is the rule that keeps them in the graph and turns a tangle of parallel proof-of-work blocks into one ordered history. Summary: GHOSTDAG is Kaspa's live blockDAG ordering rule. It is not DAGKnight, and it does not produce instant finality. The mechanism Why Kaspa needs it Problem Fast block times mean honest miners regularly find blocks within moments of each other. Old shape A single chain has to pick one branch. The losing branch's work gets thrown away as orphaned or stale. Kaspa shape A blockDAG keeps both blocks. Neither gets discarded. Ordering rule GHOSTDAG sorts the graph into a blue set and a red set, then gives every node the same procedure for ranking it. User effect Transactions show up in a block fast. Confidence that the block stays in the blue set builds as more blocks reference it. Boundary Fast inclusion is not the same as irreversibility. How final a transaction is still depends on confirmation depth and how much risk the recipient will tolerate. Common mix-ups What GHOSTDAG is not Question Answer Best wording Is GHOSTDAG live? Live GHOSTDAG is Kaspa's live blockDAG ordering rule. Is it DAGKnight? No DAGKnight is a separate, later consensus design. Does it remove finality risk? No Inclusion is fast. Confirmation confidence is still probabilistic. Does it mean unlimited TPS? No Throughput is bounded by block capacity, mempool policy, fees, and demand. Sources Check the mechanism against the primary sources Kaspa Research covers the protocol lineage, Rusty Kaspa is the implementation, the status page tracks current labels, and the finality page works through payment-confidence wording in detail. pages.text: FAQ Direct answers to common Kaspa questions The answer comes first. Check the linked status page, term, or source when the answer depends on evidence you should see for yourself. Common search Is Toccata live? Toccata activated at DAA 474,165,565. Next up: upgraded-node behavior, wallet support, explorer support, SDK support, app receipts, and actual user activity. Common search Is DAGKnight live? No. DAGKnight is a research and upgrade direction. Current mainnet consensus is GHOSTDAG. Common search Does Kaspa have smart contracts? No mature Kaspa-native programmability on mainnet yet. The near-term path runs through Toccata, then later vProgs. Common search What is GHOSTDAG? Kaspa's live rule for ordering a blockDAG so parallel honest blocks still count toward consensus. Common search Why is KAS cheaper than BTC? Unit price is the wrong comparison. Market cap, adoption, liquidity, and certainty carry the real signal. Common mistakes What needs context? Speed, TPS, finality, testnets, apps, and adoption are five separate topics, not one. Live network What is live now? Is Kaspa Proof of Work? Yes. Kaspa is mined Proof of Work, not Proof of Stake. What is GHOSTDAG? GHOSTDAG is Kaspa's live consensus rule for ordering a blockDAG so parallel honest blocks still count toward consensus. What does 10 BPS mean? Roughly ten blocks per second in the Crescendo-era network. Throughput and finality still run into their own protocol limits. Common misconceptions Short corrections for claims that spread fast Does 10 BPS prove a fixed TPS number? No. TPS depends on workload and transaction shape. Simple payments currently run roughly 2.5k to 3.4k TPS; covenant apps, ZK settlements, tokens, and vProgs each need their own measurement context. See Kaspa TPS Explained . Does 10 BPS mean 10x finality? No. Faster blocks improve inclusion and capacity. Confirmation confidence is a separate question, and it's still probabilistic. Does real-time mean instant finality? No. Real-time means fast mined inclusion and a fast user feel. Finality confidence stays probabilistic either way. Do testnet numbers count as mainnet? No. Testnets and experiments are development evidence. Mainnet guarantees need mainnet evidence. Does code activity mean activation? No. Branches, pull requests, demos, and talks show progress, not activation. Activation needs a primary release, KIP, node, or network confirming it. Does low fee usage prove adoption? Not by itself. Low fees just make experiments cheap. Adoption needs durable wallets, integrations, liquidity, apps, recurring users, and fee-paying demand. Why is one KAS so much cheaper than one BTC? Unit price and valuation are different things. Bitcoin has fewer units and a far larger market cap, and the market prices it as a proven monetary network with deep liquidity, institutional access, custody, derivatives, and a global brand. Kaspa trades more like a promising technical network that still has to prove durable adoption beyond its architecture. Could that mean Kaspa is underpriced? Only if the market is discounting future adoption too heavily. The bullish case: fast Proof of Work, Toccata, based-app development, and real products eventually create demand the market hasn't priced in yet. The skeptical case: Bitcoin already has monetary certainty, while Kaspa still carries execution, liquidity, wallet, app, and adoption risk. Does a roadmap idea belong in the headline? Usually not. Lead with what works now, then say plainly what still depends on future upgrades. Roadmap and research Still open Is Toccata live? Yes. Toccata activated at DAA 474,165,565. Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 is the current Toccata release; v2.0.0 set the activation parameters. Use Toccata status for post-activation checks. Are Kaspa smart contracts live? No mature Kaspa-native programmability on mainnet yet. The near-term path runs through Toccata: spend rules, asset rules, ZK proof checks, sequencing commitments, then later vProgs. Does Toccata allow one action across multiple apps? Only partly. Atomicity is the boundary: two transactions landing near each other is weaker than one combined operation that succeeds or fails as a unit. Toccata gives Kaspa covenant, ZK, sequencing, and based-zk foundations for fast verifiable coordination. Full app-to-app atomic actions belong to the later vProgs roadmap. Can a ZK proof prove what happened on another chain? Not by itself. A proof shows that a circuit checked against chosen inputs. A bridge or oracle-style app still needs an agreed anchor for the outside fact: a source-chain light client, finality certificate, accumulated-work view, oracle, reporter set, or challenge process. Does Kaspa need a based rollup for the first Toccata apps? No. Direct L1 covenant examples like vaults, escrow, and assurance contracts can be built on Toccata itself. A based rollup becomes relevant later for richer execution, especially where the path stays compatible with vProgs. Is DAGKnight live? No. DAGKnight is a parameterless/adaptive consensus upgrade direction. Current mainnet consensus is GHOSTDAG. Are vProgs live? No. vProgs are roadmap architecture for apps that prove richer rules while sharing Kaspa ordering. Live app infrastructure needs activation and product evidence first. Does Toccata mean external L2s are required? No. The thesis is L1-first: Toccata puts covenant and based-zk rails on Kaspa L1 itself, and apps or runtimes build on that shared ordering and payment surface. Full vProgs later target app-to-app composition beyond standalone based-zk apps. Is native Kaspa DeFi live? No. Native DeFi is still roadmap/application architecture, waiting on future foundations and tooling. Are RTD-derived oracle or TangVM flows live? No. Base RTD is Hashdag's real-time PoW framing for Kaspa. Oracles, TangVM, miner attestations, and public group-commitment markets are app-level research ideas built over Kaspa primitives, and product claims need their own implementation evidence. Does DAGKnight use observed latency? The research framing uses adversarial or worst-case latency assumptions: conditions rougher than the smooth latency seen during normal network operation. What does Solana-like mean? A cohesive, Rust-friendly developer and user experience. Kaspa L1 keeps its own execution model regardless. Comparison How should Kaspa be described? Is Kaspa just Bitcoin but faster? No. Better framing: Kaspa is Proof of Work redesigned around parallel blocks. It keeps mined security but orders competing blocks through a blockDAG and GHOSTDAG instead of picking one chain. Does Kaspa solve every scaling problem? No. The live claim is narrower: faster Proof-of-Work inclusion and confirmation dynamics through a blockDAG. Storage, node resources, fees, and future app infrastructure are all still open work. Does Kaspa require super-fast internet? Current GHOSTDAG carries latency assumptions, like other synchronous consensus systems. DAGKnight is the future research direction for removing a fixed protocol latency parameter, but it isn't live today. Does pruning make Kaspa private? No. Pruning and missing explorer history aren't privacy guarantees. UTXO state remains the consensus object, and broadcast transactions can still be observed or archived by others. Next step Next reading path If the terms above are unfamiliar, start from zero. If you just need shipped-vs-roadmap status, go straight to the status table. Start from zero Open status Keep reading Next pages Previous GHOSTDAG explained How Kaspa orders parallel proof-of-work blocks in a blockDAG, without claiming instant finality. Next Kaspa's design case How Kaspa's design maps to neutral money, self-custody, fast payment feel, and public rules people can inspect. Status Kaspa current status Live, targeted, roadmap, and research claims, sorted into plain buckets.

pages.title: Kaspa Design Case | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: How Kaspa's design maps to neutral money, self-custody, fast payment feel, and public rules people can inspect.
pages.text: Kaspa's design case Crypto earns its keep when people need one shared record and no single operator controlling it. Kaspa's bet: can Bitcoin-style Proof-of-Work security and censorship resistance run closer to real time without giving either one up? The thesis: keep Proof-of-Work security culture while making payment inclusion feel closer to real time. Start with the job Crypto is a poor substitute for most payment apps, databases, courts, or corporate platforms. It earns its place where people need neutral ownership records, self-custody, censorship resistance, programmable assets, global access, or public rules a platform can't quietly rewrite. Kaspa picks one constraint inside that frame and pushes on it: how close can decentralized settlement and coordination get to real time without abandoning Proof of Work? Crypto job Kaspa angle Status Self-custodied money Fair-launched Proof-of-Work UTXO asset with direct wallet control. Live Fast payment feel 10 BPS blockDAG gives quicker inclusion than slow PoW chains. Live, with confirmation tradeoffs One shared record GHOSTDAG orders parallel honest blocks in a DAG. Live Assets with rules Toccata activated at DAA score 474,165,565 on Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1: spend rules, asset rules, ZK hooks, sequencing commitments, and vProgs groundwork. L1 rule surface live; wallet/tooling and app evidence next Group commitments Base RTD today; RTD-derived attestations, oracles, TangVM, and public markets for shared commitments later. Base idea live; app systems still future work Kaspa focuses on latency Bitcoin proved strangers can coordinate around scarce digital money with no central operator. It pays for that with a slow block interval, chosen partly because network latency has to stay small relative to block production: a real tradeoff baked into every Nakamoto-style system, not an oversight. Kaspa comes out of the research line asking whether a Proof-of-Work network can include parallel honest blocks and still converge on one ordering. The question underneath: can more honest mining work participate in consensus instead of getting discarded as wasted collision? That claim is narrower than ordinary "faster chain" marketing: the architecture targets the block-rate/latency tradeoff directly, not vague speed. Explaining it means naming the actual mechanics: parents, mergesets, blue/red classification, blue work, and the virtual block. Parents are direct block references. The mergeset is the set of blocks incorporated around a selected parent. Blue work lets the network compare accumulated work across a DAG instead of a single chain. The virtual block gives nodes a current-state reference without pretending there's only one tip. GHOSTDAG does not make every block equal. It gives nodes a rule for ordering the graph. Inclusion and confirmation are separate claims Any fast block-producing system can get a transaction into a block quickly. That's inclusion. It says nothing about confirmation: how fast the network gives strong confidence the transaction won't reverse. Conflating the two is the most common way "fast blockchain" claims mislead. This is where fast Proof of Work makes a distinctive argument. Proof of Stake typically gets fast finality by rapidly collecting votes from staked validators, which ties confirmation speed directly to validator coordination and stake distribution. Push decentralization further and that coordination gets harder, often pushing the system toward committees or other sampling shortcuts. Proof of Work samples security a different way. A block is proof the finder out-competed the network's hash power for that round: the protocol never needs to poll a supermajority of miners before confirming anything. That decouples block-production speed from miner-count coordination. The two models also diverge on cost. Proof of Work imports external cost into consensus: electricity, ASICs, facilities, cooling, supply chains, geography, time. Proof of Stake secures the ledger with internal token ownership instead. That difference changes neutrality, issuance, attack economics, and what sovereignty even means, while PoW keeps its own energy, ASIC, pool, and regulatory exposure. Fast confirmation also depends on bounded DAG mechanics, not just raw block rate. K, finality depth, anticone finalization depth, merge depth, and BPS-scaled parameters are the safety rails that keep high block production from turning into unbounded parallelism. "10 BPS" by itself is not the claim. The honest limit: fast PoW blockDAGs change the inclusion/confirmation/decentralization tradeoff, they don't eliminate it. That narrower claim is the actual reason to study Kaspa. less stake-vote coordination Bitcoin slow inclusion, PoW confirmations Kaspa fast inclusion, PoW confirmations Ethereum PoS finality, committee sampling Solana fast UX, stake-vote finality faster inclusion RTD is the broader idea RTD stands for Real-Time Decentralization. In Hashdag's framing, it's Kaspa's core value proposition first: Bitcoin-style Proof-of-Work security and censorship resistance, with real-time confirmation feel. RTD is measured in real system time. A partially synchronous system should move as fast as the actual network allows: fast when conditions are clean, slower but still safe when the network is degraded or under attack. RTD-derived oracle, attestation, TangVM, and group-commitment flows sit a level up. Those are app-level architecture and research ideas built on top of Kaspa's high-frequency PoW sampling. The protocol supplies the base primitives, and applications define their own incentives, rules, data sources, and risk controls. Rules strangers can rely on The Oxford talk and related Hashdag framing skip past price charts and generic blockchain slogans and treat crypto as a tool for shared commitments: funding thresholds, prediction markets, internet institutions, and systems where strangers need enforceable rules without trusting one platform. The simplest version is Kickstarter-like funding: money moves only if enough people commit, and the rule is enforced by the system, not a company that can override it. Group-commitment markets extend that same idea to public goods, prediction markets, oracle resolution, or AI-agent commitments. Kaspa fits that frame because fast Proof-of-Work blockDAG infrastructure already expresses the base RTD thesis, and supports the public ordering, censorship resistance, real-time responsiveness, and open participation that markets or funding rules need. The markets, oracle mechanisms, and TangVM-style flows themselves are still research and architecture work. Live-product claims about them need shipped product evidence, which doesn't exist yet. Kaspa's base-layer direction is what makes this line of work worth tracking. Programmability, by status Kaspa's app-layer path runs through Toccata, spend rules, asset rules, Silverscript, ZK proof checks, sequencing commitments, and vProgs groundwork. Toccata activated at DAA score 474,165,565 on Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1, roughly June 30, 2026 at 16:15 UTC. Michael Sutton's April 2026 outlook explains why the original May 5 target moved. The L1 rule surface is live; wallet support, tooling, and app usage are the next evidence to watch. The mechanism: money can carry a rule forward. A vault can limit when funds move, a group payment can refund if a condition fails, and an asset can require the right controller before it moves, enforced through transaction introspection, covenant identifiers, sequencing commitments, and proof checks, all Kaspa-specific machinery. The clearest way to picture covenant-style apps is as controlled UTXO state machines. Kaspa.com Learn's smart-contract/chess walkthrough models registration UTXOs, player UTXOs, game-state UTXOs, move-routing transactions, move-application transactions, and final settlement. The point isn't chess. It's a rule-bound workflow that never turns Kaspa L1 into a global account VM. That's where assets with rules, cohesive DeFi, and apps that prove their own logic belong: built around covenants, ZK proof checks, sequencing commitments, and later vProgs. The split holds at the architecture level: L1 handles ordering, commitments, proof checks, and metadata; apps prove the richer logic around it. "Solana-like" here means cohesive developer and user experience, not shared architecture. vProgs are Kaspa-native verifiable-program architecture, not ordinary rollups wearing a different name. Current boundaries Ethereum leads today in application depth, liquidity, and developer adoption. Solana leads today in consumer app adoption and cohesive fast-app UX. Toccata's L1 rule surface is activated; native Kaspa DeFi built on top of it is still in the roadmap/application lane. DAGKnight sits in the research and upgrade lane. vProgs sit in the roadmap architecture lane. RTD-derived oracle, TangVM, and attestation flows are app-level constructions over basic Kaspa primitives. Coordination markets remain a research and architecture direction until real products and usage exist. Execution risk Architecture is not adoption. The case weakens if node-resource requirements rise too far at higher BPS, if mining or pool concentration worsens, if declining emissions aren't offset by real fee demand, if Toccata's activated rules fail to attract apps with actual usage, or if bridge/oracle systems introduce trusted bottlenecks that undercut the whole point. There's also competitive risk: Ethereum, Solana, Bitcoin L2s, stablecoin rails, and app-specific chains can win users just by being good enough for the job. Kaspa's differentiated claim has to turn into usable infrastructure, not stay a differentiated claim. The core question Proof-of-Work crypto with Bitcoin-style security and censorship resistance operating in real time, with future apps that prove their own rules built around it. That's the value proposition: a neutral shared record, pushed on speed, latency, inclusion, and group action, without giving up Proof of Work's external-cost security model. Follow the references Bitcoin Takeover S16 E41 with Yonatan Sompolinsky for the long-form Kaspa, DAGKnight, vProgs, PoW, and community-context discussion. Podscan transcript for searchable interview context. Yonatan Sompolinsky Oxford Union address for public group-commitment markets, stag-hunt framing, internet institutions, and crypto as rules strangers can rely on. Oxford Union Q&A for the AI-agent, tokenization, and network-effect discussion. Kaspa: Mining the Internet for the RTD, miner-attestation, and internet-money-layer framing. Michael Sutton vProgs talk for apps that prove their own rules, share Kaspa ordering, and keep computation minimal. Michael Sutton on Crescendo, based rollups, and DAGKnight for 10 BPS, storage controls, sequencing commitments, and DAGKnight implementation planning. hashd.ag and hashd.ag/raw for Yonatan / Hashdag writing and research framing. Where to go next The one-screen page compresses this thesis to its essentials. The comparison page shows exactly where Kaspa's lane sits next to everything else. pages.title: Where Kaspa Fits | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: Where Kaspa fits against Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, stablecoins, exchange chains, meme assets, and major smart-contract L1s.
pages.text: Crypto awareness Where Kaspa fits in crypto Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, stablecoins, exchange chains, and meme coins are not competing in the same race. Each one picked a different tradeoff and optimized for it, so "which is better" is the wrong question to start with. Start narrower: new to crypto, start with Start Here . Confused by the coin market, use the Coin Atlas . Then read the Kaspa design case . Kaspa's lane gets clearer once you separate the jobs a blockchain actually does from the jobs a token adds nothing to. Summary Different networks solve different jobs Kaspa keeps Proof of Work and a fixed-supply monetary base, the same primitives Bitcoin uses. The difference is ordering: instead of forcing every block into one linear chain, Kaspa uses a blockDAG that includes parallel blocks other PoW chains would throw away as orphans. Bitcoin has the longest track record as a store of value. Ethereum has the deepest smart-contract ecosystem. Solana has the most mature fast-app consumer environment. Kaspa is ahead on none of those today. Its claim is architectural: faster Proof-of-Work settlement now, with programmability staged in behind it. These are category sketches, not full protocol audits of each network. The table below is a routing tool, not a ranking. Comparison table Scan the tradeoff surface first Ask two questions in order: what job is this network optimized for, and does Kaspa's fast mined ordering actually change anything for that job. Network Best at today Consensus / trust shape App layer today Kaspa contrast Bitcoin Conservative Proof-of-Work monetary asset. PoW, linear chain, very conservative base layer. Limited on L1; richer activity mostly external or layered. Kaspa keeps PoW but changes the ordering shape from one chain to a blockDAG. Ethereum Smart contracts, DeFi liquidity, developer network effects. PoS with rollup-centric scaling and large app ecosystem. Live and mature relative to most crypto. Kaspa-native programmability is not live; the roadmap targets apps that prove rules around mined ordering. Solana Fast, cohesive L1 UX and active consumer apps. PoS/high-performance validator system. Live, fast, and much more mature than Kaspa's app layer. Kaspa tests fast user experience around mined PoW settlement. XRP Payment and settlement narrative. Not PoW; more institution/company-adjacent history. Not a general smart-contract ecosystem in the Ethereum sense. Kaspa is fair-launched PoW with no banking-integration thesis. BNB Exchange-linked ecosystem utility. Corporate ecosystem gravity shapes adoption heavily. Live app/token ecosystem tied to Binance network effects. Kaspa has no corporate issuer and must earn adoption without exchange-platform gravity. TRON Cheap stablecoin movement, especially USDT flows. Pragmatic payment network with a different trust and issuance model. Stablecoin usage is the main practical story. Kaspa is not yet competing on stablecoin usage; its claim is fast PoW infrastructure. "Which coin is better at everything" has no answer. The useful question is narrower: What is each network good enough for, and what tradeoff does it make to get there? Kaspa answers that as a fair-launched Proof-of-Work monetary network with a blockDAG design: fixed supply, mined settlement, same as Bitcoin, but with a different rule for what happens when two miners find a block at nearly the same time. The core mechanism, stated plainly: Keep proof-of-work, keep a fixed-supply monetary base, and let a blockDAG include parallel blocks that a single-file chain would usually throw away. That is a different bet than Bitcoin's or Ethereum's: proof-of-work competing on speed and future programmability while keeping Bitcoin's monetary and security culture intact. Bitcoin Where Bitcoin is already good enough Bitcoin wins the job when the job is simple, conservative, and monetary: the most recognized proof-of-work asset, the longest track record, and a base layer that changes as little as possible on purpose. Bitcoin is not optimized for fast consumer payments on L1, rich smart contracts, or high-frequency applications, and that is a deliberate choice, not an oversight. A ~10-minute block interval is the price of conservative settlement money. Long-term store of value Institutional reserve narratives Conservative proof-of-work exposure Settlement where speed is not the main constraint Users who prefer protocol ossification over rapid feature development Kaspa keeps the same Proof-of-Work issuance model and trades Bitcoin's single-chain rule for GHOSTDAG ordering, which is what gets mined blocks included faster. Ethereum Where Ethereum is already good enough Ethereum wins the job when the product needs programmable settlement inside the largest smart-contract ecosystem in crypto: the deepest DeFi liquidity, the most battle-tested tooling, and the broadest developer base. Ethereum's scaling answer is modular: L1 stays the settlement and data layer, execution moves to rollups. That solves throughput but creates a different problem: liquidity fragments across rollup environments, each with its own bridge, sequencer, and trust assumptions. "One chain, one experience" stopped being true the moment execution left L1. Kaspa's roadmap targets app rules closer to the base layer instead of pushing execution off-chain. That is a roadmap claim, not a shipped one. Ethereum is far ahead today in applications, liquidity, and developer adoption, and will stay ahead until Kaspa has usage evidence to point to. Solana Where Solana is already good enough Solana wins the job when the product needs fast, cheap, monolithic crypto UX today: one execution environment, low fees, and confirmations fast enough that users don't notice they're on a blockchain. That cohesion is Solana's real advantage. Users, developers, and liquidity all concentrate in one environment instead of spreading across bridges and rollups. Kaspa's speed argument is a different mechanism than Solana's. Fast inclusion means a transaction enters a block quickly. Fast confirmation means the network gives strong confidence the transaction won't reverse. Solana gets confirmation speed from proof-of-stake validators voting; Kaspa is testing whether fast Proof of Work can get comparable confirmation confidence without needing the protocol to collect explicit votes from a supermajority of stake on every block. Solana's tradeoffs run the other way: proof-of-stake consensus instead of mined issuance, a more actively optimized base layer, and a different security culture than the hard-money, mined-into-existence story Bitcoin and Kaspa both tell. Today, Solana is far ahead in apps and users. Kaspa's claim rests on architecture and roadmap, not current ecosystem size. Kaspa Where Kaspa fits Kaspa borrows from three places at once: Bitcoin's proof-of-work money, Solana's fast monolithic UX, and Ethereum's programmable application layer. It does not replace any of them today. Bitcoin is still the dominant PoW store-of-value asset, Ethereum still has the deepest smart-contract liquidity and tooling, and Solana is still the clearest example of fast, low-fee, high-activity L1 UX. Kaspa's claim is that the combination itself is rare: proof-of-work issuance, fixed supply, fast block production with parallel block inclusion, an everyday payment feel, and a path toward application UX that stays in one place instead of fragmenting across rollups the way Ethereum's did. "Fast" in that claim means three things at once: block rate, confirmation confidence, and decentralized miner participation. The open question is whether fast Proof of Work can deliver all three without collapsing into the same validator-coordination problem proof-of-stake systems face. The mechanics that make this a different category, not just a faster Bitcoin: GHOSTDAG ordering, blue work, bounded anticones, virtual state, pruning, UTXO commitments, transaction mass, and storage-mass pricing. Each one exists to keep a high-rate PoW DAG understandable and validatable, not as decoration. Stated as narrowly as the evidence allows: Proof-of-work infrastructure with faster confirmation goals. That means fast inclusion plus improved confirmation dynamics, not instant finality. Proof-of-work can feel faster without stopping being proof-of-work; that's the bet, and it's narrower than it sounds. Major categories Compare by category Stablecoins: USDT and USDC Stablecoins already solve dollar movement: payments, trading collateral, remittances, exchange liquidity, and dollar access where local banking is unreliable. The tradeoff is trust: issuers, reserves, banking access, compliance, and redemption all sit behind the token. Stablecoins answer: how do I move dollars on crypto networks? Kaspa answers: can proof-of-work money move at internet speed? BNB and exchange-linked ecosystems BNB's strength and its risk are the same fact: it works because Binance works. An exchange-linked ecosystem can move fast, subsidize activity, and attract users quickly, but the value proposition is tied to one company's continued dominance. BNB answers: what can a large exchange ecosystem power? Kaspa answers: what can a fair-launched proof-of-work network become without a corporate issuer? XRP and payment/settlement networks XRP targets fast settlement and institutional payment corridors. Both XRP and Kaspa get discussed in payment terms, but the architectures diverge at the root: XRP is not proof-of-work, and Kaspa carries no company-led banking-integration story. XRP answers: can a dedicated settlement asset serve payment corridors? Kaspa answers: can decentralized proof-of-work offer fast settlement without abandoning mined issuance? TRON TRON already solves cheap stablecoin movement: most of its usage is USDT transfers. Kaspa is not competing with TRON on stablecoin throughput or app adoption; it isn't in that race yet. TRON answers: where can users move stablecoins cheaply today? Kaspa answers: what a fast proof-of-work base layer looks like as it matures. Dogecoin and Shiba Inu DOGE and SHIB run on culture first. Dogecoin adds proof-of-work heritage and unusual staying power; SHIB runs on meme liquidity and community gravity. Neither is competing on architecture, so neither is in Kaspa's lane. DOGE/SHIB answer: can culture itself become liquidity? Kaspa answers: can proof-of-work architecture support a monetary and application network? Cardano, Avalanche, Sui, TON, Hedera, Polkadot, and other smart-contract L1s Most large smart-contract L1s start as programmable platforms and compete for developers, apps, liquidity, and users. Kaspa starts from the opposite end: proof-of-work money and blockDAG consensus first, with programmability layered on afterward. Most smart-contract L1s answer: can we build a better app platform? Kaspa answers: can proof-of-work itself be upgraded into high-speed programmable infrastructure? Chainlink Chainlink provides oracle infrastructure, a different category from base-layer money entirely. As Kaspa's application ecosystem develops, oracle infrastructure becomes something it needs, integrates with, or builds an alternative to. Chainlink answers: how do smart contracts get external data? Kaspa answers: what base layer are those future applications anchored to? Source notes Sources for the comparison Bitcoin whitepaper for Bitcoin's original peer-to-peer electronic cash and proof-of-work chain framing. Ethereum scaling docs for rollup-centric scaling and decentralization tradeoffs. Solana homepage for Solana's high-performance positioning and ecosystem framing. XRPL developer portal repository , BNB Chain , and TRON for how those projects present payment paths, exchange-linked ecosystems, and stablecoin-heavy networks. rusty-kaspa , rusty-kaspa releases , Kaspa KIPs , and Kaspa Research for Kaspa implementation, proposal, and protocol-design evidence. pages.h1: The main Kaspa ideas, in order
pages.description: An accessible map of the main Kaspa ideas synthesized from KASmedia, Kaspa.com Learn Kaspa, and primary Kaspa sources.
pages.text: Learning path The main Kaspa ideas, in order Kaspa clicks faster when the ideas arrive in order: money, blocks, DAGs, ordering, speed, tradeoffs, status, then apps. Public learning material helps get there. Status-sensitive claims still need checking against primary technical sources. Reading intuition: start with what a shared record actually does, then move from live mechanics into the application lanes, but only after the base design makes sense. Reader path Learn in this order Start with one shared record. Who owns what, who can spend it, and who gets to change the rules. Understand Proof of Work. Mining, Sybil resistance, costly ordering, and an external clock. See the chain bottleneck. Honest blocks arrive in parallel, but a single chain forces one path. Learn five DAG words. Parent, past, future, anticone, and mergeset. Learn GHOSTDAG's live job. Blue/red classification and ordering by accumulated work. Separate inclusion from confirmation. Fast blocks are not instant finality: they're two different claims. Understand storage and pricing. Pruning, UTXO commitments, mass, and finality are part of scaling, not afterthoughts. Put ideas in the right lane. Toccata is activated on mainnet. vProgs, DAGKnight, RTD, and Proof of Useful Work each carry a different status. The short ladder Seven core ideas 1. PoW is the base culture Kaspa keeps mined issuance, external work, and Nakamoto-style ordering as first principles. The fair launch and costly external security process separate it from permissioned identity or stake voting. 2. The bottleneck is single-file ordering Bitcoin forces one chain of blocks. Kaspa accepts that honest miners find blocks in parallel and orders that parallel work instead of discarding most of it as waste. 3. GHOSTDAG is the live ordering rule The DAG structure alone is not the invention. Classifying and ordering the blocks inside it is the hard part. GHOSTDAG uses selected parents, mergesets, blue/red classification, and blue work to keep the blockDAG coherent. 4. Fast means inclusion, confidence, and capacity Fast inclusion is a transaction entering a block quickly. Fast confirmation is reversal risk dropping quickly. Kaspa's speed argument rests entirely on keeping that distinction straight. 5. Storage has to be engineered High throughput means nothing if nodes can't keep up with it. Pruning, UTXO commitments, MuHash, finality depth, transaction mass, and storage mass are the parts of the security story that make throughput sustainable. 6. Toccata activated the base app-layer surface Toccata activated at DAA score 474,165,565 on Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1: covenants, Silverscript, KIP-10, KIP-20, KIP-21, and ZK verification hooks are live on L1. vProgs extend that surface and remain roadmap. Wallet support, tooling, and repeat app usage are the evidence still building on top of activation. 7. The broader target is group action RTD framing starts with real-time Bitcoin-style PoW security, then points beyond payments toward attestations, oracles, public funding contracts, and markets where no single referee should control the rules. Parallel upgrade tracks DAGKnight and vProgs are different lanes Both get discussed together because both point beyond today's GHOSTDAG/Crescendo network, but they're solving different problems on different timelines. Track What it changes Current public code signal Status lane DAGKnight Consensus ordering and latency assumptions. DAGKnight is the adaptive-successor direction after GHOSTDAG. Application runtime claims need separate app-layer evidence. rusty-kaspa/dagknight has March 22, 2026 commits around free search, ranking, conflict-zone logic, tie-breaking placeholder, and UMC majority coverage. Research / prototype branch; live-mainnet evidence pending vProgs Proof-producing apps that use Kaspa for ordering, commitments, payments, and proof checks. kaspanet/vprogs had an April 15, 2026 ZK implementation burst: RISC0 backend, ZK VM, provers, ABI, codec, and Sparse Merkle Tree work. Roadmap / early framework; production app paths pending Split: DAGKnight changes how Kaspa orders blocks under changing network conditions. vProgs let apps prove richer logic while Kaspa stays the shared ordering and proof-checking anchor underneath. Source context Long-form background Open long-form background map Distributed-systems foundations The Understanding GHOSTDAG series and related theory posts start below Kaspa entirely: Byzantine agreement, PoW, heaviest-chain rules, GHOST, safety, liveness, confirmations, selfish mining, DAGs, topological sorting, PHANTOM, and GHOSTDAG. The takeaway: Kaspa isn't a marketing shortcut around consensus. It comes out of a long attempt to generalize Nakamoto consensus. Fast PoW and finality KASmedia's interview recaps separate raw block rate from confirmation confidence, and reinforce PoW as an external clock and leaderless sampling mechanism. Crescendo and Rusty Kaspa Crescendo and Rusty Kaspa material shows 10 BPS depended on Rust engineering, parallel validation, pruning improvements, mempool work, sync/exchange integration, and storage controls, not just a parameter flip. Toccata and covenants Toccata activated on mainnet at DAA score 474,165,565 on Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1. The Toccata/Covenants++ coverage stays concrete when it names the actual pieces: spend rules, transaction introspection, covenant IDs, Silverscript, native assets, ZK proof checks, and sequencing commitments. Full native DeFi claims still need shipped app, liquidity, and user evidence built on top of the activated rule surface. vProgs and ZK architecture The vProgs material points toward apps that prove their own logic: L1 stays focused on ordering, commitments, proof checks, and metadata, while richer app logic runs in proof-producing environments. That's different from both ordinary rollups and global L1 execution. RTD, oracles, and group commitments Hashdag's RTD writing explains why Kaspa people keep talking about real time. The base claim is Bitcoin-style PoW security with real-time confirmation feel; the later claim is public rules that people, software, markets, and eventually AI agents can rely on. Fee markets and resource pricing The fee-market and storage-mass material frames fees as incentives that protect the shared record from spam, UTXO bloat, and mispriced externalities. Wallets, custody, and user reality KASmedia's wallet and interview material grounds the tech in actual use: hot/cold wallets, seed phrases, custodial vs. non-custodial tradeoffs, point-of-sale tools, community infrastructure, and why self-custody still needs better UX. What Learn Kaspa adds The concept library fills in the mechanical vocabulary BlockDAG relationships Past, future, anticone, parents, mergesets, selected parents, and virtual blocks are the vocabulary that stops a reader from imagining Kaspa as one chain with faster timestamps. It isn't one chain. Ordering and work Blue score, blue work, k-clusters, K, and blue/red classification are how Kaspa decides which blocks contribute to the consensus structure and how accumulated work gets compared across a DAG instead of a line. Finality and pruning Finality depth, anticone finalization depth, pruning depth, first-order pruning, second-order pruning, archival nodes, and full nodes are how the network cuts stored history without losing the ability to validate it. Timing and difficulty DAA score, DAA window, timestamp validation, and past median time keep timing and difficulty coherent on a high-rate PoW DAG without leaning on naive wall-clock assumptions. Transaction validation Transaction selection, transaction validation, transaction mass, storage mass, and mempool behavior exist because high throughput still needs collision-aware selection and spam-resistant pricing. Speed alone doesn't solve either. Programmability building blocks KIP-10, KIP-20, KIP-21, opcodes, covenants, and smart-contract explainers show the direction of Kaspa apps: scripts inspect transaction context, preserve covenant lineage, track app lanes, and prove rules without every app becoming global L1 execution. Concrete covenant patterns The Smart Contracts / chess walkthrough shows a UTXO app as constrained state transitions: registration, player identity, game state, move routing, move application, and settlement. The strongest examples prove continuation state, rejected paths, sibling authority, and timeout behavior, without claiming a live app ecosystem that doesn't exist yet. Smart contracts without the shortcut Programmability has layers Layer Plain-English role What not to claim Native script Bitcoin-like spending conditions, signatures, multisig, timelocks, and deterministic validation. Not a general-purpose app VM. KIP-10 introspection Scripts can inspect transaction context, which makes richer UTXO spending rules possible. Not full app-state management by itself. Covenants / covenant IDs UTXOs can be constrained to evolve through specific patterns or lineages. Not automatic DeFi, identity, or legal enforcement. ZK proof checks and sequencing commitments Apps can prove computation and track relevant activity without every proof depending on the whole DAG. Not the same thing as vProgs being live: vProgs remain roadmap. Silverscript / vProgs direction Developer-facing tools and apps that prove rules could make the system usable for richer applications. Not an existing Ethereum- or Solana-scale ecosystem. Source context: Kaspa.com Learn Kaspa: Smart Contracts . Status-sensitive details should still be checked against KIPs, releases, and core developer posts. Corrections Common phrasing fixes Weak explanation Better explanation "Kaspa is Bitcoin but faster." Kaspa is a Proof-of-Work blockDAG that includes and orders parallel honest blocks instead of discarding them as ordinary orphans. That's a different consensus structure, not just a speed dial. "10 BPS solves everything." 10 BPS needs the surrounding mechanics to mean anything: GHOSTDAG ordering, BPS-scaled parameters, pruning, finality, transaction selection, and resource pricing. "Treating DAGKnight as current mainnet behavior." DAGKnight is a major parameterless/adaptive consensus direction still in the roadmap and research lane, not mainnet behavior today. "Kaspa already has native DeFi." Toccata's L1 rule surface activated at DAA score 474,165,565 on Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1: that's a real base to build on. Native DeFi itself still needs wallet support, tooling, liquidity, and shipped apps built on top of it. "Pruning means missing history or weaker nodes." Pruned full nodes still validate correctly when pruning proofs, finality, UTXO commitments, and retained state are designed right. Archival nodes and full nodes serve different roles, neither is "weaker" by default. "Fees are only about miner revenue." Fees and mass rules also price resource externalities: compute, temporary storage, and permanent UTXO-set growth. "RTD just means faster payments." RTD is Kaspa's real-time PoW framing first. It also supports future attestations, ordering, public commitments, oracles, and markets that don't need one trusted referee. Attribution Use the map, then check the sources Treat this as the compact guide, not the final word. The Sources & Reference Map keeps attribution, reference links, and supporting site files in one place. pages.text: Glossary Kaspa glossary Short, precise definitions for Kaspa-specific terms, linked into the longer explainers. Core mechanics Live-network terms Proof of Work Miners spend real computation to propose blocks. Kaspa keeps this Bitcoin-like foundation intact. Related: BPS , GHOSTDAG , DAGKnight UTXO An unspent transaction output: a spendable coin chunk. Kaspa spends UTXOs; Ethereum edits account balances instead. Related: pruning , MuHash , covenant BlockDAG A graph of blocks where multiple honest blocks can exist in parallel, instead of every block forced into one line immediately. Related: GHOSTDAG , anticone , mergeset , selected parent GHOSTDAG Kaspa's live consensus rule for ordering the blockDAG so parallel work still counts toward consensus. Related: blue/red blocks , blue work , selected parent , anticone Selected parent The parent block that defines the main ordering path through the DAG. Not the same thing as Bitcoin's longest chain. Mergeset The set of past blocks a new block pulls into view: how parallel work gets folded into the ordering. Anticone Blocks that sit in neither a block's past nor its future. Nodes need an anticone rule to order these consistently. Blue / red blocks GHOSTDAG marks well-connected blocks blue and less-compatible ones red, for ordering and security accounting. Blue work Accumulated proof-of-work weight carried by blue blocks. It's how Kaspa compares competing DAG histories. Blue score A blockDAG progress marker built from blue blocks in the selected-parent chain. Explorers and APIs use it for ordering and range queries. DAA score A Kaspa progress marker nodes and APIs expose. Builders use it for block ranges, timestamp estimates, and lock-time reasoning. Virtual block The conceptual current tip nodes use to reason about the present state of the DAG. Speed and storage Scaling terms BPS Blocks per second. Kaspa runs at 10 BPS in the current era. Throughput and finality are separate claims with their own measurement assumptions. Fast inclusion A transaction gets into a block quickly. Fast confirmation Confidence that a transaction won't be reversed rises quickly. Not the same thing as appearing in a block quickly. Finality depth The threshold past which old history counts as settled under the protocol's assumptions. Pruning Discarding old block data that ordinary nodes no longer need for current validation. Related: archival node , MuHash , UTXO Archival node A node that keeps full historical data for explorers, audits, and historical queries. MuHash A compact commitment tool used to verify UTXO-set state and keep pruning safe. Transaction mass Kaspa's measure of a transaction's resource cost. Storage mass A cost model that makes UTXO/state growth pay for the burden it puts on the network. Sompi The smallest unit of KAS. One KAS equals 100,000,000 sompi. APIs return amounts as strings so software doesn't lose precision. Hosted API An API run by a provider outside your own node or indexer. Fine for quick reads and prototypes; production apps need key handling, rate-limit handling, and a reliability plan. API key A credential sent with hosted API requests, usually in a header like x-api-key . Keep it out of client-side code and public repos. Rate limit A provider rule that caps request volume. Apps should read rate-limit headers, cache stable data, batch where possible, and back off on 429 responses. Cursor pagination Fetching long lists in stable chunks. Address history endpoints use it so apps can walk through many transactions without one huge response. Accepting block The block that accepted a transaction into ordered history. Acceptance data is evidence, but apps still need confirmation and reorg-handling rules on top of it. Roadmap terms App and research terms Toccata The activated hard-fork track for spend rules, asset rules, ZK proof checks, sequencing commitments, and vProgs groundwork. It activated at DAA score 474,165,565. Related: covenant , ZK verification , sequencing commitment , vProgs Covenant A rule that limits how a coin or asset can be spent later: the basis for vaults, escrow, and simple app state. Silverscript A higher-level scripting direction built on Kaspa's covenant and programmable-UTXO path. ZK verification Checking a proof that computation was done correctly, without re-running that computation on L1. Sequencing commitment Lets an app track the activity lane it actually cares about, instead of forcing every proof to depend on the whole DAG stream. vProgs Apps that prove their own logic around Kaspa, while L1 stays focused on ordering, commitments, verification, and metadata. Related: ZK verification , sequencing commitment , covenant DAGKnight A parameterless/adaptive consensus research direction. Not current mainnet behavior. Related: GHOSTDAG , BPS , fast confirmation RTD Real-Time Decentralization: Hashdag's framing for Kaspa's core edge, Bitcoin-style PoW security and censorship resistance operating in real time. Oracle and TangVM ideas are downstream extensions of this. Related: Proof of Work , DAGKnight , fast confirmation Proof of Useful Work A speculative research direction where mining work might also perform useful computation. Not live Kaspa functionality.
